items.title: story: our own OIDC/SAML/SSO identity provider
items.body:
## User story

As the operator of our own services, I want one self-hosted identity provider issuing OIDC + SAML SSO for our own services — pm-stack, the mcpx and Desktop Commander doors ([#13404 — Desktop Commander front door endpoint](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13404)), OpenChamber, fleet surfaces — so that sign-in across our estate runs on our own identity instead of a patchwork of third-party IdPs and per-service arrangements.

Motivation:

- One identity: the same person, service, and policy across every service, instead of a separate account story per service.
- Our own trust anchor: signing keys and certificates issued from our own PKI, under our own control, instead of trusting a vendor's keys for our own estate.
- No per-service vendor dependency: adding a service means registering a relying party with our provider, not adopting another third-party IdP or inventing a one-off sign-in scheme.

Done at the story level looks like: our provider is the sign-in path for at least one service of each class in the acceptance criteria below, its signing keys come from our PKI and can be rotated without breaking sign-in, and a new service can be onboarded by configuration against our provider rather than by choosing a new identity vendor.

This story does not start from a blank page. It is the story-level frame over the SSO program that already exists — parent issue [#9077 — parent SSO program issue itself](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/9077) and its children — plus the PKI foundation and the SAML scope, which the existing program does not cover. The "Prior work and references" section below is the map; the slice plan builds on those pieces rather than re-specifying them.

## Scope + acceptance criteria

- [ ] PKI foundation exists: root CA, an issuing intermediate, and cert-generation tooling (Slice 1).
- [ ] OIDC discovery + JWKS signing works: the provider publishes its discovery document and a JWKS signed from PKI-issued keys.
- [ ] SAML IdP metadata + signing works: the provider publishes signed SAML IdP metadata and signs SAML responses.
- [ ] At least one relying party from each class signs in end-to-end: a web app, and a CLI/API surface.
- [ ] Signing-key rotation is demonstrated: a new signing key is published and trusted, and the old key is retired, without breaking sign-in.
- [ ] Operators can issue and revoke service certificates from the PKI.
- [ ] Provider accounts bind to pkgs/id accounts via the binding ceremony in [#2852 — hosted provisioning SSO ID binding](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/2852) (recorded as acceptance debt in the provider child issue, not an afterthought).

## Prior work and references

Search record (2026-11-23, GitHub issue search over developing-today/code, counts confirmed from the search API): `oidc` 222 hits, `saml` 4, `sso` 71, `"identity provider"` 73, `idp` 20, `oauth` 170, `login` 301, `auth` 1185. The `login`/`auth` counts are broad and noisy; the relevant hits are below.

**Plain findings first:**

- **SAML is new ground.** All 4 `saml` hits are the github-backup estate mirror and GitHub-org SAML access — no prior SAML IdP design, issue, or design record found. The SAML scope in this story is genuinely new work, not a re-specification.
- **Number corrections to the original brief for this story:** the Google federated-login issue is [#13412 — Google federated login door work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13412), a child of #9077. [#12412 — console gate whole public hostname](https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/12412) is a closed PR (the pm-stack console as the gate for the whole public hostname), related to the Access wiring but not itself a Google-login issue. And [#8299 — id roles capability ceiling config](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/8299) is pkgs/id role configuration (capability ceilings, delegation bounds), not mcpx work — the mcpx ceiling/session line is [#1902 — mcpx daemon ceiling caller lowers](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/1902), [#1950 — mcpx OAuth authorization conformance work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/1950), and the mcpx book's identity chapter (below).

### The existing SSO program — #9077 and its children

- [#9077 — parent SSO program issue itself](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/9077) — SSO for fleet services: GitHub/Google/Microsoft login gated to Drew + a devtoday OIDC provider with roles + account linking. This story's OIDC half is that program, framed at story level and extended with PKI + SAML.
- [#13409 — minimal devtoday OIDC provider standup](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13409) — standard OIDC issuer (code + PKCE), JWKS + key rotation, Drew-only allowlist enforced in the provider, #1253 role claims, no id keypair custody in the login path.
- [#13411 — GitHub federated login door work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13411)
- [#13412 — Google federated login door work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13412)
- [#13414 — Microsoft federated login door work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13414)
- [#13415 — account linking flow with history](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13415) — one account, every door, with retained identity history.
- [#13416 — first consumer proving full loop](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13416) — first consumer integration (PM stack) proving the full loop.
- [#13417 — fleet SSO provider decision note](https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/13417) — the decision note PR for #9077; it settles the pkgs/id question (see the design questions below). Open at filing time; its design record is `doc/2026-11-23_design_fleet_sso_9077.md` on its branch until merged.
- [#9086 — hosted editions consume SSO design](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/9086) — hosted editions are relying parties consuming #9077; tenancy accounts aligned with #1253 roles.
- [#1253 — one identity across the stack](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/1253) — SSO propagation from the public entry into every layer; the four-role model (owner / orchestrator / agent / read-only) is the consumer-side contract the provider's claims must carry.
- [#1182 — dashboard behind Cloudflare Access design](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/1182) — the settled Access model for the pm-stack entry; the existing door this provider eventually stands behind.
- [#9605 — stack token minting exchange work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/9605) — stack-token minting + agent token-exchange under #1253; how an entry session becomes per-layer tokens.

### pkgs/id — the existing identity system

- [#2056 — ID platform expansion epic home](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/2056) — the ID program epic; pkgs/id is Drew's identity system (Iroh-key identity, id-caps capabilities, directory, groups).
- [#2852 — hosted provisioning SSO ID binding](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/2852) — external SSO identities bound to pkgs/id accounts (spec source #2258); slices 1–2 landed, 3–4 open at last record in #9077.
- [#5684 — identity login delegation design work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5684) — identity, login & delegation: key custody, security-code recovery, pseudo-login identities. Its custody questions are unresolved, which is part of why the provider does not start inside id.
- [#2060 — key recovery versus SSO loss](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/2060) — the standing rule from the key-recovery investigation: SSO authenticates a person to an account record; it never rebinds an identity key.
- [#2380 — keyset authorization log identity substrate](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/2380) — device keys, revocation, and bindings as signed records; the revocation/rotation substrate Slice 5 builds on.
- [#8299 — id roles capability ceiling config](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/8299) — roles as first-class world config: capability ceiling, delegation-lifetime bounds, grant/revoke as audited events. The id-side role/ceiling model the provider's roles must not silently diverge from.

### Doors, mcpx, and fleet token auth — worked examples and neighbours

- [#13404 — Desktop Commander front door endpoint](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13404) — Worker front door, Access gate, laptop bridge.
- [#13488 — OAuth front door shipped implementation](https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/13488) — merged PR: OAuth 2.1 front door for hosted MCP clients (`pkgs/desktop-commander/worker/src/oauth.ts`). The in-house worked example of the OAuth pattern.
- [#12417 — Google OAuth client creation task](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/12417) — the Google OAuth client for pm.security.cab; the concrete Google-side wiring the Access door runs on today (closed).
- [#12412 — console gate whole public hostname](https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/12412) — closed PR: the pm-stack console is the gate for the whole public hostname.
- [#1950 — mcpx OAuth authorization conformance work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/1950) — mcpx as OAuth client / resource server. Per `doc/fleet/mcpx-oauth-authorization-server.md` (decision 2026-10-28), mcpx does **not** embed an authorization server — it points at external ones. This provider is the external server it points at.
- [#13657 — mcpx public endpoint front door](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13657) — mcpx public endpoint with an OAuth/Google-SSO front door and machine bearer; a first-class relying party candidate for this provider.
- [#1902 — mcpx daemon ceiling caller lowers](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/1902) — the capability-ceiling mechanism (daemon sets, caller may lower, never raise) that provider-issued policy/session claims must respect.
- [#5343 — laptop agent resident execution design](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5343) and [#5362 — queue secrets brokers laptop design](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5362) — the fleet/laptop-agent token-auth line: brokered, token-gated laptop services reached only through the session proxy. The machine-to-machine auth pattern the provider's CLI/API relying parties should align with, not replace casually.
- [#9158 — fleet CA canonical secrets model](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/9158) — fleet-ca canonical secrets model, provider adapters & custody policy; adjacent to Slice 1's PKI — the CA program links #9077 and does not absorb it (per its design record below), and this story returns the favour.

### Design records (repo `doc/`)

- `doc/2026-11-23_design_fleet_sso_9077.md` — the #9077 decision note (via PR #13417, on branch until merged): settles separate-minimal-provider-first, with an explicit fold path into pkgs/id.
- `doc/2026-10-30T22-45-00Z_design_hosted_provisioning_sso_binding.md` — hosted provisioning + SSO→ID binding spec (#2258 line): Google SSO authenticates the account; the Iroh root key is the identity.
- `doc/2026-10-28T23-34-14Z_investigation_cloudflare_workers_fit/` — §4: Google SSO on Workers and binding a Google identity to an ID identity; "SSO is the door; the ID key remains the identity"; custodial keys rejected.
- `doc/2026-10-29T11-28-18Z_investigation_key_recovery_hosted/` — key recovery for hosted users; verified at the time that pkgs/id contained no Google/OIDC/OAuth/WebAuthn code — all SSO content was specification.
- `doc/2026-11-10T23-58-00Z_design_pm_stack_identity/` — the #1253 design record: Access JWT at the entry, short-lived stack tokens per layer, roles in the aggregator registry, "the central OIDC provider (#9077)".
- `doc/2026-11-01_design_id2046.md` + `doc/2026-11-01_design_id2283.md` — hosted-edition identity designs; they record an unresolved conflict with the Oct 30 SSO spec (`binding_id` vs `sub` as the store key) that the design pass must reconcile, not rediscover.
- `doc/fleet/mcpx-oauth-authorization-server.md` — mcpx embed-vs-point-at decision: hybrid, point-at-first; mcpx never issues tokens, it validates other issuers' tokens via JWKS.
- `doc/2026-11-13T01-34-11Z_design_fleet_ca_credentials_secrets/` — the fleet CA / credentials / secrets program: its note links #9077 as an adjacent relying-party/identity program it does not absorb; its spec (§27) already compares Keycloak / Authentik / Kanidm / Zitadel for a standalone SSO platform — the build-vs-adopt design pass starts from that comparison, not from zero.
- `doc/2026-11-12T19-10-07Z_design_keyset_authorization_log/` — the #2380 keyset/authorization-log design.
- `pm-stack/console/README.md` — records today's wiring plainly: `google.access-sso` OAuth client secrets, the Access sign-in method, and "the central OIDC provider (#9077)" as the intended provider.

### The four books

- **id book** (`pkgs/id/book/`): `concepts/identity-directory.md` (Identity, the directory and groups), `concepts/capabilities.md` (Capabilities, ceilings and providers), `design/identity-directory-groups.md` (identity, directory, groups and delegation), `design/hosted-editions.md` (hosted and serverless editions), `design/capabilities-providers.md`. This is where id's identity model is written down as a book, and the fold-path design must be written against it.
- **mcpx book** (`pkgs/mcpx/docs/`): `spec/identity.md` ("Who an MCP request is from"), `compare/register/auth.md` (the authorization register: OIDC discovery, PKCE, issuer checks), `decisions/0007-elicitation-identity.md` (elicitation binds no user identity), and the auth rows of `spec/conformance-matrix.md`.
- **fleet book** (`pkgs/fleet/book/`): `concepts/proxy.md` (Proxy, sessions and recovery) and `reference/queue-dispatch.md` are the closest chapters — the fleet book covers sessions and tokens as transport, and **no dedicated SSO/identity chapter was found in the fleet book**.
- **atlas book** (`pkgs/atlas-search/book/`): `design/fleet-and-id-integration.md` and `design/access-evolution.md` touch ID integration and access evolution; **no prior dedicated identity, federation, or sign-in design was found in the atlas book**.

### Sandbox-side notes

- `~/memory/topics/id-program-2026-10-28.md` — Drew's ID program directive: the Workers edition signs in via Google SSO, Google `sub` is the SSO key, custodial keys rejected.
- Standing operator practice (memory, 2026-10-24): SSO-first sign-ins for Drew's own service accounts — operator practice, not IdP design, listed here so the two are not conflated.
- No SAML material was found in the sandbox notes either — consistent with the GitHub search: SAML is new ground on every front searched.

## Open design questions — options and chosen defaults

Chosen defaults below are recorded under Drew's decision posture: prefer options, "both" where both can coexist, and the more capable option over the most locked-down or most basic. Where a prior decision already exists, it is recorded as the chosen default rather than re-decided.

### 0. Relationship to pkgs/id — the central question

pkgs/id **is** an identity system (Iroh-key identity, capabilities, directory, groups; epic #2056). Any new provider has to state its relationship to it:

- **Option A — Same system:** pkgs/id itself becomes the OIDC/SAML provider.
- **Option B — A layer over it:** a thin OIDC/SAML protocol layer whose accounts and keys are id accounts and id keys throughout.
- **Option C — Deliberately separate first, with a fold path:** a separate minimal provider now; provider accounts later bind to id accounts via the #2852 ceremony, with an explicit path for the provider to fold into id.
- **CHOSEN: Option C — separate minimal provider first, explicit fold path into pkgs/id.** This is the decision already recorded in the #9077 decision note (PR #13417; Drew may override per §5 of that note). Reasoning, from #9077's own evidence: no OIDC surface exists in pkgs/id, #5684's key-custody model is unresolved and more exotic than a conventional issuer, #2852's binding slices 3–4 are open — while fleet services need boring, standard OIDC first. Two standing constraints bind whichever option the design pass lands on: no id keypair custody in the login path (#13409), and SSO never rebinds an id key (#2060).

### 1. Build vs adopt

- **Option A — Hand-build:** build the IdP ourselves on our own components.
- **Option B — Adopt-and-package:** adopt an existing IdP core (e.g. Keycloak-class), package and run it ourselves, fronted by our own PKI.
- **CHOSEN: Option B — adopt-and-package.** Identity protocols are high-risk to hand-roll; our differentiation is the PKI and the integrations, not the protocol code. Note for the design pass: this must be reconciled with Question 0's "separate **minimal** provider" — the fleet CA program's spec already compares Keycloak / Authentik / Kanidm / Zitadel (see Prior work), and the pass must show the adopted core can stay minimal (Drew-only gate, #1253 role claims, PKI-issued signing keys) rather than assuming it.

### 2. Where it runs

- **Option A — Laptop-hosted only:** run the provider as a service on the laptop.
- **Option B — A fleet surface only:** run the provider on a fleet surface.
- **Option C — Both, laptop primary:** run it laptop-hosted first, with a fleet surface as the same provider's second home / reach path, laptop primary.
- **CHOSEN: Option C — both, laptop primary.** It starts where our execution already lives, without closing off a fleet home when reach needs it. (Open sub-question for the design pass: the hosted/Workers edition line under #9077's relatives is a third home candidate — the pass should address it explicitly rather than this story guessing.)

### 3. How relying parties integrate

- **Option A — Direct per service:** each service is configured directly for OIDC/SAML against the provider.
- **Option B — Via the door Workers:** the existing door Workers act as relying-party proxies in front of services.
- **CHOSEN: Both A and B.** They can coexist — direct config where a service supports it well, door Workers as proxies where a service needs a door in front of it. PR #13488's Commander door is the worked example of B; #9086 is the design home for hosted editions consuming the provider directly (A).

### 4. Signing-key rotation

- **Option A — Manual ceremony:** rotation is a deliberate, manual operator ceremony.
- **Option B — Automated rollover:** automated rollover with overlapping JWKS publication, so old and new keys are both trusted during the changeover.
- **CHOSEN: Option B — automated rollover with overlapping JWKS publication.** Overlap makes rotation routine instead of an outage risk, which is what makes rotating often practical. This is already in #13409's scope ("JWKS + key rotation"); Slice 5 proves it rather than designing it from scratch.

### 5. Relationship to the existing Access / Google SSO wiring

Related, not duplicated here: [#13412 — Google federated login door work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13412) and [#13411 — GitHub federated login door work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13411) / [#13414 — Microsoft federated login door work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13414) (the federated logins under #9077), [#12417 — Google OAuth client creation task](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/12417) (today's Google client for pm.security.cab), and [#13404 — Desktop Commander front door endpoint](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13404) (the Commander OAuth door).

- **Option A — Rip-and-replace:** remove the existing Access/Google wiring and replace it with this provider in one move.
- **Option B — Stand behind the doors:** keep the existing doors and wiring in place, and make this provider the identity standing behind those doors, taking over from Google as the upstream identity over time.
- **CHOSEN: Option B — stand behind the doors, not a rip-and-replace.** The doors our services already use keep working; what changes is whose identity is behind them. This matches #9077's own shape: GitHub/Google/Microsoft stay as federated logins **into** our provider, gated and linked to one account — Google goes from being the identity to being one door into ours.

## Slice plan — in dependency order

1. **Slice 1 — PKI foundation:** cert-generation tooling + root CA + issuing intermediate. *Executed in parallel by the PKI foundation work, 2026-11-23, alongside the filing of this story.* Builds alongside the fleet-ca program ([#9158 — fleet CA canonical secrets model](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/9158) and its design record above) rather than re-specifying a CA model.
2. **Slice 2 — Signing keys:** signing keys for OIDC (JWKS) and SAML, issued from the PKI — the keys [#13409 — minimal devtoday OIDC provider standup](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13409) already scopes as "JWKS + key rotation", now sourced from our PKI instead of provider-local generation.
3. **Slice 3 — The provider itself:** the provider stood up per #13409 + the #9077 children (#13411 / #13412 / #13414 federated logins, #13415 account linking), publishing OIDC discovery/JWKS — **plus SAML IdP metadata + signing, which is new work with no prior design (see Prior work) and needs its own design slice in the design pass.**
4. **Slice 4 — Per-service integrations:** [#13416 — first consumer proving full loop](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13416) (PM stack) first, the Commander door pattern (PR #13488) for Worker-fronted services, and mcpx as a pointing-at relying party per its authorization-server decision ([#1950 — mcpx OAuth authorization conformance work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/1950), [#13657 — mcpx public endpoint front door](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13657)) — one per service class first, then the remaining services.
5. **Slice 5 — Rotation + revocation drills:** demonstrate signing-key rotation (overlapping JWKS, per Question 4) and certificate revocation end-to-end, building on the keyset/authorization-log substrate ([#2380 — keyset authorization log identity substrate](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/2380)) instead of inventing a parallel revocation story.

## Closing note

This issue is the design-mill intake (starter issue) for the identity program, so it can route into a full design pass next. The design pass's first job is reconciliation, not invention: the #9077 decision note, the `binding_id` vs `sub` conflict recorded in the id hosted-edition designs, the build-vs-adopt vs minimal-provider tension in Questions 0–1, and the SAML scope, which has no prior art in the repo.

items.body:
Follow-on to #7948 (queue task 14308): the mcpauth failover machinery has landed (identity list config, soft/hard classification, rotator with durable state + rotation logging, App installation-token minter, pool resolves the current identity's credential at connection start). Two pieces remain before the github namespace fails over live:

1. **Daemon call-path wiring**: when a `tools/call` result from the github server carries a GitHub API soft block (the error text embeds the API status/body), translate it to `mcpauth.APIError`, run the call through `Rotator.Do`, respawn the github instance with the rotated identity's env, and retry — so the calling session never sees the soft block. Hard blocks surface unchanged.
2. **Live activation**: enroll the three GitHub App identities' private keys in the mcpx secret store (by name only), add the `failover` block to the github server's auth config with the user token last, and set the rotation state path.

Acceptance: a staged low-limit identity in front of the real one shows a session-visible success on a forced soft block in the live namespace, with the rotation log line naming both identities; hard-block behaviour unchanged.

items.body:
Follow-up from the key-recovery investigation on #2060 (doc: `doc/2026-10-29T11-28-18Z_investigation_key_recovery_hosted/`, §4/§7 and §11). Parent epic: #2056.

## Ordering (triaged 2026-11-03)

Slices per the investigation's §11; this issue is the **umbrella** for the export/server-backup/rotation remainder, not one implementation task:

- **Slice 1 — `id key export` / `id key import` passphrase-wrapped envelope: #2279** (open, queued, not started). Prerequisite for everything below; do not build a second envelope format here.
- **Seed-phrase (BIP39-style) export/restore** — unique to this issue; shares #2279's KDF/envelope module; dispatch after #2279.
- **Server-side backup blob + rate-limited blinded unwrap (OPRF)** — design decision first (no OPRF or backup-blob code exists at main); ciphertext-only server storage; depends on slice 1.
- **Restore-forces-rotation flag** — needs the keyset log substrate in #2380 (device keys, revocation, bindings).
- Guardian/social recovery is #2382; issuer key rotation is #2804 (different scope).

## Problem
If the only ID key is lost and no device survives, there is no recovery path that keeps the server from holding keys. The investigation recommends encrypted backups where the server holds ciphertext only.

## Proposal
1. Seed-phrase (BIP39-style) export/restore of the identity secret in the `id` CLI — zero server involvement; doubles as the hosted-edition exit ramp.
2. Passphrase-wrapped backup stored server-side (hosted edition): memory-hard KDF, and a rate-limited blinded unwrap (OPRF-style) so the server can throttle guessing without learning the passphrase or the key.
3. A backup-restored key is flagged until a keyset rotation retires it (restore may follow theft).

## Acceptance
- [ ] `id` CLI can export a seed phrase and restore an identity from it, with tests.
- [ ] Server backup format + unwrap throttling designed and documented; server never sees plaintext key material at any step.
- [ ] Restore flow forces/prompts rotation of the restored key.

items.body:
## Why

The PM stack still depends on the laptop as the only runtime/data host. Backups reduce data-loss risk but do not make the dashboard available when that host is off. Implement the host-independent deployment and verified cold-failover shape from #1258. Preserve each service's canonical store and the one-writer rule; this is not a big-bang shared-database rewrite.

## Scope

- Move the aggregator, Kaneo/PostgreSQL, Grist, and Pad runtime to the approved cluster/alternate host as their canonical deployment; keep the laptop as an operator/development client.
- Keep aggregator-owned mutable data on the Supabase `muse-dev2` path defined by #3142/#941; retain service-owned Kaneo, Grist, and Pad stores in their approved persistent homes.
- Configure persistent storage, backup/restore integration, and health/freshness reporting so no unique record is held only in laptop-local JSON or Docker volumes. Coordinate with #1514 and #3869; do not duplicate their backup implementation.
- Keep the stable Cloudflare Access URL. Route it to the active host; store host credentials by name in Bitwarden/SOPS and do not commit plaintext secrets.
- Implement explicit single-writer fencing and a cold-restore runbook; do not add automatic multi-writer failover.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A documented deployment target and ownership map exists for aggregator, Kaneo, Grist, and Pad; each service has one named canonical data home and one active writer.
- [ ] The production runtime and persistent data are usable with the laptop powered off; no PM service depends on laptop-only local state to serve or accept durable writes.
- [ ] Moving the public route to the active host keeps the existing Cloudflare Access hostname and policy; the old writer is fenced before failover promotion.
- [ ] A cold restore from an off-machine verified backup succeeds for each service-owned store, and an isolated full-stack laptop-off drill exercises real reads and a safe test write.
- [ ] Measured RTO/RPO are recorded in `doc/pm-stack/restore-drills/YYYY-MM.md` and meet or explicitly revise the #1258 proposals (4h core RTO; 15m aggregator mutable state; 1h Kaneo/usage/link state; 24h Grist/Pad).
- [ ] Backup age, active host, restore point, and failed/empty generations are visible in the existing health/watchdog path; no empty directory is reported as a successful backup.
- [ ] Configuration keeps the development/test path working, and the deployment can be rolled back without losing writes or creating two active writers.

## Boundaries

- #3142 owns the phased aggregator schema migration; #941/#4642 own identity/provenance semantics. This issue consumes those contracts, not redesigns them.
- #1514 owns the application-database backup routine; #3869 owns silent empty-day/container-name failure handling.
- #1218 owns GitHub Project audit export. GitHub remains canonical for GitHub data.
- No secrets, copied production data, or raw private records in this repository or drill reports.

Parent: #1184. Design: #1258.

items.title: design: transport adapter contract — declarations, levels, asymmetric routing (multi-transport head)
items.body:
# Design: the transport adapter contract (multi-transport head design)

Parent epic: #13926 — Multi-transport reach: any protocol as a carrier. Direction recorded on #13752 (comment 7118605020). This is the programme's head design: everything else in the epic plugs into the contract defined here.

## 1. Problem + context (with evidence)

Drew's direction (2026-11-23): the P2P / ID / fleet stack should be reachable over many alternate transports and proxied alternate systems — Spritely-style relays, Tor, Noise, ActivityPub, ATProto, email, MQTT, HTTP/REST, MCP, IRC, Zulip, Slack, Discord bots, Gopher, Gemini, telnet beside SSH, physical media — each at a declared level (read / bidirectional / write-capable / sync-equivalent), with **asymmetric send/receive paths as a first-class requirement** ("send over carrier pigeon, receive over fax" is a design requirement, not a joke).

Today every path we have invented its own shape, because no contract exists:

- The **bridge** (#13895) is an HTTP note transport with class/name addressing and token-gated send — its own addressing, its own gating.
- The **mcpx door** (#13657, live) is an MCP endpoint with its own gate/proxy rules.
- **Email** exists in the #13752 design as a bootstrap carrier for signed tickets — introductions only, no message contract.
- **Sneakernet bundles** (#13889) carry signed data + grants for ID — a sync-shaped path designed inside the ID-graph programme only.

Four instances, four shapes. Each new carrier added ad hoc multiplies integration and security-review cost, and nothing today can express "reachable at read level over X, writable over Y, replies come back over Z" — the asymmetry Drew requires.

## 2. Goals and non-goals

**Goals**

- One adapter contract that every carrier family in the epic's inventory can be expressed in without special cases.
- Every adapter **declares** its properties up front (machine-readable), including its level per direction.
- Asymmetric routing as a core property of the message envelope, not an adapter feature.
- Identity on every path binds back to the fleet CA / ID identity — or the gap is explicitly declared (proxies).
- Levels are **proven live** before they are recorded as held.

**Non-goals**

- Building all adapters now (this design sequences them; most are later children of the epic).
- Replacing or altering the primary broker/iroh path (#13752 pilot stays broker-ticket-first).
- Anonymity guarantees of our own (a Tor adapter carries Tor's properties; the contract claims none).
- Solving platform terms-of-service questions for bot proxies — the contract records the trust/custody facts; acceptability is decided per adapter.

## 3. Alternatives considered

- **Do nothing; keep adding transports ad hoc.** Cheapest this quarter; the four existing instances show the cost curve — every new path re-invents addressing, gating, and metering, and asymmetry stays inexpressible. Rejected.
- **One central gateway service translating everything.** Single custody and trust point; contradicts the federated/stateless direction of the relay work and #13752. Rejected.
- **Adopt a multi-transport library wholesale (libp2p-style).** Strong for overlay transports; silent on email, chat proxies, federation protocols, and physical media. Kept as a component choice *inside* individual adapters, not as the contract.
- **A thin contract: declaration + routing core, adapters independent (chosen).** The contract standardises only what must agree — declarations, envelope, routing, gating, metering — and leaves each adapter's internals free.

## 4. The contract

### 4.1 What every adapter must declare

A machine-readable **adapter declaration** (the registry entry):

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `name`, `version` | Adapter identity |
| `shape` | `transport` or `proxy` (see §4.4) |
| `addressing` | How a peer/user is named on this carrier, and the mapping to fleet-CA / ID identity |
| `levels` | Level held **per direction** (send / receive), from §4.2 |
| `delivery` | At-most-once / at-least-once; ordering guarantee; whether causal metadata survives; latency class; size limits; offline behaviour |
| `identity_binding` | `cryptographic` (end-to-end, both ends are our stack) / `mapped` (proxy-held mapping table) / `none` (public read-only) |
| `capability_gating` | What capability a sender needs at each level; how revocation reaches this path |
| `metering` | What is counted (messages / bytes / actions) and where the counter lives |
| `custody` (proxies only) | Who holds the platform credentials; the platform trust statement; the translation boundary (§4.4) |

### 4.2 The four levels, defined precisely

- **read** — the adapter delivers inbound messages/observations to the stack. No outbound path exists or is used. (Delivery semantics still matter: read over email is durable and complete; read over a chat system is an editable, deletable stream. The declaration says which.)
- **bidirectional** — messages flow both ways over this adapter. Not necessarily one connection: an email adapter declaring SMTP-out + IMAP-in is one adapter at bidirectional.
- **write-capable** — the stack can originate *state-changing actions* on the far side (post, publish, execute), not merely messages. Distinct from bidirectional because writes carry authority: this level requires the capability-gating declaration to be non-empty.
- **sync-equivalent** — the adapter can carry the data plane's full sync protocol (per #13779's compositions) with convergence intact: causal metadata survives, bulk transfer works, withholding/replay behaviour is declared. Reference instances: sneakernet bundles (#13889), iroh-class transports.

### 4.3 Asymmetric routing rules

1. Every message envelope carries an explicit **reply route** (adapter + address). A sender never assumes the reply arrives on the path it sent on.
2. The routing core selects the send adapter and the expected receive adapter **independently**; a route is a (send, receive) pair, either side of which may be any registered adapter at a sufficient level.
3. Delivery receipts, where an adapter supports them, travel the declared reply route.
4. Timeouts and failure handling are per-direction: a dead send path says nothing about the receive path.
5. Level checks apply per direction against the *pair*: e.g. a write sent over a write-capable adapter may legitimately receive its result over a read-level adapter.

### 4.4 Transport adapter vs proxied alternate system

Drew listed both shapes deliberately; the contract treats them differently.

- A **transport adapter** carries the stack's own messages end-to-end. The far end is another instance of our stack (or a peer implementing the same contract). Identity binds cryptographically at both ends; the carrier sees framing/ciphertext, not content or authority.
- A **proxied alternate system** terminates at a platform we do not control — a Discord/Zulip/Slack bot, an ActivityPub server. The proxy speaks the platform's protocols in the platform's identity model; messages are *translated* at the proxy boundary; the far end may be a human, not our stack. Identity binding is a **mapping table held by the proxy**, not a cryptographic property of the path. The platform can read, retain, rate-limit, and revoke.

Consequences in the contract: a proxy must additionally declare `custody` (who holds the platform credentials), the **translation boundary** (which message types survive translation, and what is lost), and a **trust statement** (what the platform operator can see and do). Gating differs: a transport adapter gates by capability end-to-end; a proxy gates *at the proxy*, whose own authority is its platform identity plus its mapping table — so a compromised proxy can forge within its platform scope, and proxy declarations must state that scope as a ceiling.

### 4.5 Security analysis per level

- **read:** inbound injection and spoofing are the risks. Per the #13752 ticket doctrine, the carrier is untrusted: authenticate the payload (signatures, CA binding), never the channel. A read adapter must not let carrier-side metadata (sender fields, headers) become identity claims.
- **bidirectional:** adds session confusion and cross-path correlation, plus **downgrade**: a peer reachable at sync level on a strong path must not be trickable into accepting write authority asserted over a weaker path. Authority claims are verified against the capability, not the path — and the path's declared level caps what may be *accepted* from it.
- **write-capable:** adds authority amplification and confused-deputy risk (worst at proxies, §4.4). Revocation propagation must be declared: on a store-and-forward path (email, sneakernet), a revoked capability may still be in flight — the receiving side verifies at receipt time, never at send time.
- **sync-equivalent:** adds full-state exposure to the path and convergence attacks (withholding, replay, selective delivery on store-and-forward media). Bundles verify before merge (#13889's rule); replay windows and ordering claims live in the `delivery` declaration.

### 4.6 Data model

Three durable objects: the **adapter declaration** (above), the **route** (a named (send-adapter, receive-adapter, address-mapping) triple a peer or service is reachable by), and the **envelope** (payload + reply route + capability reference + per-path metadata the declared delivery semantics require). No other shared state; adapters keep their own internals.

## 5. Proposed first-adapter order (grounded in what exists)

1. **HTTP/REST, by formalising the bridge** (#13895) — code exists; proves the declaration shape against a real adapter at near-zero build cost.
2. **Email** — already designed as a bootstrap carrier in #13752 (Delta Chat pattern is researched); store-and-forward makes it the natural first proof of asymmetric routing.
3. **MCP, by formalising the mcpx door** (#13657) — live today; validates the contract against a request/response tool protocol rather than a message protocol.
4. **MQTT** — first true pub/sub bus; small, well-understood; its QoS levels stress-test the delivery-semantics vocabulary.
5. **Sneakernet bundles** — rides #13889's D4 design; becomes the sync-equivalent reference instance.
6. **IRC as the first proxied system** — simplest chat shape, relay-friendly, no platform gatekeeper; then Zulip / Slack / Discord bots under the proven proxy rules.
7. **Federation protocols (ActivityPub, ATProto)** — largest surface; their native identity models must be reconciled with the CA binding deliberately.
8. **Overlay/relay transports (Spritely-style Noise XK relays, Tor)** — deepest work; builds on #13752's own roadmap.
9. **Gopher / Gemini / telnet** — small, well-specified; cheap wins that prove less about the contract, so they are opportunistic (any free lane) rather than sequenced blockers.

## 6. Build slices (dependency-ordered; each sized for one lane/session)

- **S1 — Contract + declaration schema + registry.** The §4 contract as a dated design record in doc/ plus a machine-readable declaration schema and a registry home. *Acceptance:* the four existing instances (bridge, mcpx door, email-bootstrap, sneakernet) are each expressed as declarations with no special cases; schema validation runs in CI.
- **S2 — Routing core.** Envelope with explicit reply route; independent send/receive adapter selection; per-direction level checks. *Acceptance:* loopback test adapters demonstrate the pigeon/fax case in tests — send via adapter A, reply via adapter B — plus downgrade rejection (§4.5).
- **S3 — Bridge formalised as the HTTP adapter.** *Acceptance:* bridge registered with its true levels; existing behaviour unchanged; metering counters emitted.
- **S4 — Email adapter.** *Acceptance:* live round trip between two stack identities over email only; cross-adapter asymmetric proof (email out, HTTP in) passes; revocation verified at receipt.
- **S5 — MCP adapter formalisation.** *Acceptance:* mcpx door expressed as a declaration; a tool call routed through the contract's envelope.
- **S6 — MQTT adapter.** *Acceptance:* pub/sub round trip; declared QoS mapping honoured; offline queueing matches the declaration.
- **S7 — Proxy shape proven with IRC.** *Acceptance:* custody/translation/trust declarations written and reviewed; read + bidirectional live; write off by default and gated when enabled.
- **S8 — Sneakernet adapter formalisation** (with #13889). *Acceptance:* bundle round trip declared and proven sync-equivalent; verify-before-merge enforced.

Follow-on families (federation, overlays/Tor, Gopher/Gemini, telnet, Zulip/Slack/Discord) are filed as children of #13926 once S1–S8 evidence exists, in the §5 order.

## 7. Rollout + rollback

The contract is additive: nothing existing changes behaviour. Adapters join by registering a declaration; an adapter is disabled by removing its registration (one flip, mirroring the provider enable/disable rule). Rollback for any slice is deregistration; the primary broker/iroh path is untouched throughout.

## 8. Verification plan

- A **conformance test kit** from S2 onward: every new adapter runs the same suite — declaration validation, per-level live proof, the asymmetry test, metering check — before its levels are recorded as held.
- Each slice's acceptance criteria (above) are verified live, with the proof recorded on the slice's issue.
- Security checks from §4.5 are test cases, not review comments: downgrade rejection (S2), receipt-time revocation (S4), proxy scope ceiling (S7).

## 9. Open questions (each with a named decider)

- **Q1.** Does the contract live at the fleet layer, the ID layer, or a shared library both consume? — **Decider: Drew** (on Archer's recommendation; the four instances span both layers today).
- **Q2.** May a proxied system ever hold sync-equivalent? (Recommendation: no — proxies cap at write-capable.) — **Decider: Drew.**
- **Q3.** Metering: per-adapter counters only, or unified into the fleet/PM metering plane? — **Decider: Archer** (implementation detail within the existing metering direction).
- **Q4.** Telnet: in scope only behind a relay/overlay, never plaintext on an uncontrolled segment? — **Decider: Drew.**
- **Q5.** Federation identity (ActivityPub/ATProto): fleet-CA cross-certification, or mapping-table treatment like proxies? — **Decider: Drew.**

## Links

Epic #13926 · transport design #13752 · P2P synthesis #13779 · ID-graph epic #13880 · sneakernet D4 #13889 · bridge #13895 · mcpx door #13657 · ID wire-format neighbour #5674

items.title: impl(id): keyless-custody login — OIDC account-pointer binding and OPAQUE password login over a client-held ID key

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

items.body:
## Summary

Implement the keyless-custody login chosen by the #5885 feasibility record and assigned to parent #5684 to file: **OIDC (Google) as an account-pointer binding and OPAQUE (RFC 9807) for username/password, both over one random, client-generated, client-held ID signing key.** The authorizer never possesses or can use the user's ID signing key.

Design of record:
- Parent synthesis: `doc/2026-11-23T20-55-00Z_design_id5684_identity_login_synthesis/` (#5684), especially §4 (signed-hash construction), §5 (feasibility matrix), §11.
- Feasibility + invariants: #5885 decision record (2026-11-08).
- Genesis artefact it builds on: #5884 `SetupStatement` (`doc/2026-11-08T23-17-06Z_design_id_setup_ceremony/`).
- Custody variants it serves: #5887 (b, user-held blob), #5889 (d, pseudo-login grants).

## Scope

1. **Login binding enrolment:** client signs the `"id/login-binding/v1"` binding statement (ID public key, auth issuer + subject hash or OPAQUE account identifier, custody profile, recovery commitment hash); authorizer verifies and stores the public key, statement, and signature. Binding updates require a signature from the existing ID key or the #5888 recovery threshold — an authenticated OIDC session or a password reset is never sufficient.
2. **OIDC flow:** authorization-code flow with PKCE; ID Token validated (issuer, audience, signature, expiry, nonce); `(iss, sub)` used as the account pointer only. Login success fetches ciphertext artefacts; it never by itself authorises an ID operation.
3. **OPAQUE flow:** an audited OPAQUE implementation for username/password; the random ID key is wrapped client-side under a key derived from the RFC 9807 `export_key`; the server stores the OPAQUE registration record and ciphertext only. The server OPRF seed is handled as high-entropy secret material (name only; never in code, logs, or this repo's artefacts).
4. **Challenge verification:** for ID-authorised operations (login acceptance where the ID key is required, new-device enrolment), the authorizer issues a fresh nonce/audience/expiry-bound challenge; the client-held ID key signs; the authorizer verifies against the bound public key. New-device enrolment additionally names the requested pseudo-login scope in the signed challenge (composition with #5887 §4.3 and #5889).
5. **Composition with existing code:** `pkgs/id/src/key_envelope.rs` already provides the local Argon2id/XChaCha20-Poly1305 passphrase envelope; reuse it for the wrapped-key storage rather than introducing a parallel envelope. Current `AccountSignedUp`'s bearer-secret key reconstruction is explicitly **not** a precedent for this work (#5885).

## Invariants (test oracles — from #5885)

1. The authorizer never receives the unwrapped ID private key.
2. Auth success alone never registers/replaces an ID key or expands delegation.
3. Every key-binding/recovery mutation is signed by the current key or an explicit recovery threshold.
4. Server-stored backup is ciphertext, and its offline-guessing assumptions are disclosed in user-facing copy.
5. Password reset and OIDC-account recovery are never represented as identity recovery.
6. Delegation stays least-privilege, expiring, revocable, with pseudo-login provenance preserved in raw records (full delegation implementation is the separate #5889 slice; this issue must not mint standing delegations outside it).

## Non-goals

- The custody-variant implementations themselves (setup ceremony #5884 §13, variant (a) signing service, variant (b) blob UX, recovery codes #5888, grants #5889, management UX #5890) — named as the parent synthesis §11 programme; this issue is the login layer they compose with.
- Acting as an OIDC *provider* (that is #13658's workstream, a different direction).

## Filing note (queue coverage)

Filed by lane felix from the #5684 parent synthesis (queue task 21487), per the tracked next action in #5885's decision record. Enqueued to the code pilot queue in the same pass by the filing lane.

items.title: feat(id): server-side identity backup per #5033 decision (#7360)
items.body: Implements issue #7360 (task 13046, lane code-x): the server-side identity backup from the #5033 design decision, as a new `pkgs/id/src/backup.rs` module. ## What lands - **Record** keyed by `H(pub) = SHA-256(identity public key)` holding exactly the #5033 item-2 field set (envelope bytes, envelope SHA-256, blob size, upload/download timestamps, monotone upload epoch, throttle counters, `restore_epoch`, deletion tombstone). `BackupRecord::stored_field_names()` is pinned by a test to the decision's list, so a new stored field fails CI until the decision is amended. - **Upload**: envelope bytes + `Sign_identity(H(pub) || envelope_sha256 || epoch_be)`; signature verified against the named public key, non-increasing epochs rejected, only a valid higher-epoch upload overwrites. The blob is the `key_envelope` v1 envelope byte-for-byte (108 bytes, validated shape on upload); the server never sees a passphrase. - **Download**: per-identity budget of 10/hour and 50/day counted with weighted fixed windows in the `abuse.rs` limiter shape; refusals carry retry-after. Per-IP/global limits stay with the endpoint layer's `AbuseEvaluator`. - **Delete**: signed at the record's current epoch; ciphertext + counters dropped, only the tombstone (`H(pub)` + final epoch) remains; replaying the pre-delete signed upload cannot resurrect it. Account deletion purges the tombstone. - **Restore**: client restore recovers the key from passphrase + downloaded envelope using only the existing `key_envelope::decrypt` path (wrong passphrase fails locally, no server signal). Download-for-restore increments `restore_epoch` and notifies bound devices; the restored key is not authoritative for new group epochs until notifications are confirmed. **No rotation flag** is introduced (#2380 owns that representation). - **Client create**: reuses `key_envelope::encrypt` exactly, with a weak-passphrase warning at creation per item 3's guessing-cost analysis. ## Tests (each names its oracle — the #5033 decision items) - Stored field set equals the item-2 list; no rotation field. - Bad signature / equal / stale epoch rejected; higher-epoch signed upload replaces the blob. - Malformed envelopes (length, magic, version) refused with the named error. - The 11th download in an hour and the 51st in a day are refused with retry-after; a proptest checks the budget invariant (admitted per fixed window ≤ limit) over arbitrary monotone interleavings. - Restore round-trip recovers the key; wrong passphrase fails locally. - Restore increments `restore_epoch`, notifies bound devices, blocks authoritativeness until confirmation. - Signed delete removes ciphertext; the pre-delete signed upload replay does not resurrect; tombstone purge works. Scope note: this is the backup record/endpoint logic at the `pkgs/id` library layer (store, signature/epoch/budget enforcement, client create/restore helpers). HTTP wiring into a running server endpoint composes these functions with the existing `abuse::AbuseEvaluator` per-IP/global limits. Closes #7360 --- Open in [code]smith · Need help on this PR? Tag @codesmith-bot with what you need.

items.title: Design + build: fleet connect — explicit transport selection, sessions, and drop semantics

labels.name: kind/design
labels.description: A design proposal (design-architect): multi-step, phased, decision-bearing

items.body:
## Design + build: `fleet connect` — explicit transport selection, sessions, and drop semantics

Origin: Drew's questions, 2026-11-14. Epic: #5412. Builds on #5343
(laptop-agent), #5697 (`fleet proxy ssh`), #5972 (fallback connection
mode), and the session semantics of the file-transfer build (sibling
issue filed the same day).

### Verified current state (2026-11-14) — what Drew asked to confirm

Three ways to reach the laptop exist today, chosen by *which tool you
invoke*, not by a flag:

1. **Agent exec** (`laptop-agent.py`, the day-to-day path; the Rust
   `fleet laptop-agent` domain is still a registry stub — exit 69,
   "implementation lands in a later step of epic #5412"). Commands run
   as argv directly on the laptop, **no shell** unless `--shell` is
   passed (then a login `bash -lc`). Environment is the daemon's
   systemd-user-service environment (plus the login profile under
   `--shell`) — nothing from the caller's environment crosses. **There
   is no stdin channel at all**: interactive input during a run is
   impossible on this path, which is exactly why stdin-carrying shapes
   fall back to SSH. Transport is HTTP over pooled CONNECT tunnels
   through the session proxy (warm call ~0.39–0.45 s; cold CONNECT
   ~1.8 s — all traffic hairpins the NYC DERP relay).
2. **Detached agent jobs** (`run` / `poll` / `kill` / `jobs` on the same
   daemon). Jobs persist server-side: spool files under
   `~/.local/state/laptop-agent/jobs/` on the laptop survive client
   death, disconnection, and sandbox restarts; `poll` resumes output by
   byte offset (client offsets in `~/.cache/laptop-agent/`). This is
   the one place a session/resume model already exists.
3. **Real SSH** (`laptop-ssh-real.sh`, or `fleet proxy ssh` in the
   binary since the 2026-11-11 refresh): full SSH over an HTTP CONNECT
   ProxyCommand, connection-multiplexed (ControlMaster, ControlPersist
   600 s; sshd MaxStartups raised to 200 after the 2026-10-25 root
   cause). Real shells, real PTY, real stdin/stdout/stderr streaming,
   port forwards, the laptop login environment. Drew's belief is
   correct: this is the only path with true interactive sessions today.
   The shim (`laptop-ssh.sh`) auto-routes: exec-shaped calls go to the
   agent; interactive / forwards / stdin-carrying calls go to real SSH.

Drop semantics today, per path:

- Agent **exec**: a client disconnect deliberately *reaps* the remote
  command (own process group, TERM→KILL; fixed 2026-11-10, #5343) —
  nothing is buffered for later pickup; a hiccup loses the run.
- Agent **jobs**: the job keeps running and its output spools to disk;
  reconnect and `poll` from the last offset. Buffer limit is effectively
  disk; no replay cap is specified.
- **SSH**: a drop kills nothing server-side (sshd owns the process) but
  there is no output replay — whatever printed while you were gone is
  gone unless the program itself logged it. `timeout` on the SSH path
  bounds only the local wait.
- The sandbox has **no inbound path at all**: no SSH in, no HTTP in.
  Every connection is initiated from the sandbox side or rendezvoused
  through the session proxy / brokers. (Confirmed 2026-11-14.)

### What to design and build

1. **One surface, explicit method.** `fleet connect` wraps all three
   paths with `--method exec|ssh|job|auto`. `auto` codifies the shim's
   current heuristics (stdin data or PTY or forwards → ssh; detached →
   job; else exec). Callers can always force a method — Drew: "is there
   a way to actually flag and choose the SSH connection method versus
   the other?"
2. **A session model across paths.** Generalize the daemon's job spool
   into named connect sessions: `fleet connect session <id>` attaches
   (replays output from offset, like `poll` does today), `fleet
   connect sessions` lists live/recent sessions with metadata (owning
   context id — see the context-propagation design filed the same day —
   command, host, started, state, bytes buffered). Define per-path
   buffering limits and what happens at the cap. Exec-path sessions
   should gain the job path's survive-the-client property *without*
   losing the 2026-11-10 guarantee that an abandoned run does not
   orphan forever: a bounded grace window, then reap.
3. **Stdin decision.** Either the daemon grows a stdin channel (making
   exec interactive-capable), or the routing rule "stdin ⇒ SSH" is
   made permanent and documented as the contract. Pick one on evidence;
   today it is an accident of implementation.
4. **tmux: settle it in writing.** For the SSH path, tmux on the laptop
   IS the attach/detach answer (SSH carries the terminal — there is no
   HTTP attach method and none is needed). For the agent path, jobs +
   spool already cover it. Decide whether a managed tmux pattern
   (named sessions per context id, listable, swept when stale) is
   documented, tooled, or deliberately left manual — and make sure
   anything started under tmux is cleaned up. On the sandbox, Muse's
   own exec sessions already provide the equivalent; do not build a
   second one.
5. **Inbound-less hosts (future, recorded — not ruled out, not a
   priority).** A queue task that instructs a host to open a *reverse*
   connection to a named endpoint, after which that endpoint can drive
   the host's environment. Design space only in this issue; spin out if
   it ever becomes real.
6. **Direct node-to-node (future shape).** Nodes with full network
   access may later SSH directly with per-node client certificates
   under a shared CA, every connection logged under the cert identity,
   with the proxy/coordinator pool as the universal fallback (routing
   by command, load, or session stickiness). The sandbox's network
   idiosyncrasies must keep working automatically underneath all of
   this — the fallback path is the compatibility floor, not a legacy
   mode.

### Acceptance (design phase)

- [ ] Decision record covering items 1–4 with the measured numbers
      (warm/cold per path, batch behaviour, throughput) in one table.
- [ ] Build issues split out for: the `fleet connect` surface, the
      session list/attach surface, and the stdin decision's winner.
- [ ] #5972's fallback-mode scope reconciled with this design (one
      answer, not two).

items.title: Atlas program — full investigation, next-steps design & build-out (program tracking)
items.body:
# Atlas program — full investigation, next-steps design & build-out (program tracking)

Drew's directive (2026-11-23): dig into the **full Atlas system** and design the next steps —
integrate all data sources with automatic ingest; improve query planning; integrate search for
fleet and for ID; MCP and programmatic access; more search characteristics on top of Snowflake;
reranking; a recommender; and everything else the investigation surfaces.

## Ground truth (verified 2026-11-23)

- Program epic #8983. Canonical store: laptop Turso/libSQL `~/atlas/turso-atlas/data/atlas.db`
  + 29 topic shards. Last verified census (2026-10-31, #3125): 18,325 sessions / 122,124
  messages / 107,639 chunks; the monolith has since grown to ~7.3 GB **without a verified
  recount** — consumer-facing counts are frozen at the October publish.
- #3125 phases 1–2 landed (12,092 CAS objects interned, ~2.6 GB, verify OK); phases 3–4 open.
- Production embedding model: `Snowflake/snowflake-arctic-embed-m-v2.0`, 768 dims; vectors are
  plain BLOBs — `vector_top_k` does not work on them; semantic search is an exact cosine scan
  (~4 s). Legacy BGE-small space coexists. Second-embedder evaluation open (#9092).
- Retrieval: hybrid FTS + vector, **RRF fusion only — no reranker in the serving path**.
  Query-planner flags (spell/query-class/rewritten) accepted but unimplemented
  (#9092/#5773/#5774). #12900 thread 1 landed; thread 2 (multi-client) is Drew's open question.
- Evaluation: golden-311 v3 + held-out 54, ablation harness (#5741), standing programme #8627.
  Feedback capture exists with no ranking consumer. Recommender: design only (#9140, #9109
  Part C); no candidate generation exists.
- Ingest is manual/script-driven (only schedule = daily backup); the target source list is
  #9097 Workstream E; sweep runner #7969 unbuilt.
- Sensitivity: corpus tiers public/internal/secret vs client ceilings
  shareable<personal<local-only<secret-bearing, enforced server-side. **#8479 is open: the 638
  secret-bearing chunks also live in the production monolith — the tier boundary does not
  currently hold outside the shard set** (purge-vs-reclassify is Drew's decision).
- Census: 57 open `epic/atlas-program` issues.

## Workstreams

A. Automatic ingest of all data sources (pipeline: CDC/hooks + reconciliation sweeps,
classification before promotion, tombstone purge across all stores).
B. Query planning (classifier → transforms → routed retrieval → fuse → rerank; planner flags
made real).
C. More search characteristics on top of Snowflake (MRL two-resolution index, learned sparse,
late interaction, metadata pre-filtering with tier as a security boundary, ANN path to replace
the 4 s scan, second-embedder decision).
D. Reranking (cross-encoder over fused top-50–200, golden-set-gated per corpus; BGE-Reranker-v2-m3
default candidate; feedback loop wired in).
E. Recommender (single-user signals: profile centroid, session co-occurrence, recency/frequency,
graph neighbours; more-like-this / related / resurface surfaces).
F. Fleet + ID search integration (freshness for `fleet search`; #6062 publication format +
projectors #11182–#11186 + #9109 Part C — ID's first live query path).
G. MCP + programmatic access (one retrieval core; MCP/REST/CLI surfaces; versioned API contract
from atlas-proto; #8625 cross-client acceptance; Worker cache TTL #6805).
H. Evaluation & quality programme (golden set from real traces, per-stage metrics, CI gates).
I. Book + issue map (below).

## Deliverables

1. An **Atlas book in bookwright form**, published on the existing code-repo Pages site under
   `/code/atlas/`, with a DOC-01-style docs-sync contract.
2. **An issue-by-issue map of ALL Atlas issues**, prioritized in best working order, with all
   blockers marked on the issues and in the list.
3. Designs landed by PR for every workstream; implementation PRs merged wherever unblocked.

## Operating rule

The prompt (posted as the first comment on this issue, and added to the repo by the starter PR)
is a **starting point, not a stopping point**: expand until everything possible is done, review,
repeat. Many parallel agents across analyze/research/design/document/implement workstreams.

Related: #8983, #3125, #9097, #9134, #12900, #6062, #9109.

items.body:
Split from #2381 (encrypted identity backup) as the design-first half. The local envelope half is #2279; the seed-phrase half stays on #2381.

## Problem
#2381 proposes a passphrase-wrapped identity backup stored server-side, with a memory-hard KDF and a rate-limited *blinded* unwrap (OPRF-style) so the server can throttle guessing without learning the passphrase or the key. Nothing of that exists at main `048da81f1`:

- No backup blob format anywhere in `pkgs/id/src` (`grep -rln "backup"` hits only `world_doctor.rs`, `repl/input.rs`, `currency_poc/tests.rs`, `web/routes.rs`, `cli.rs`).
- No OPRF or blinded-unwrap primitive anywhere in `pkgs/id/` or `doc/` (`grep -rli "oprf\|blinded"` → no matches).
- The identity key is still the raw file `KEY_FILE = ".iroh-key"` (`pkgs/id/src/lib.rs:314`).

Implementing this without a recorded decision would invent a wire format, a server-side key-custody posture and an unwrap-throttling protocol in one PR.

## What this design must settle
1. **Blob format** — AEAD + KDF versioned envelope (reuse #2279's header shape rather than defining a second one), keyed by identity-public-key hash; server stores ciphertext bytes only.
2. **Server-side custody posture** — restate that the server never holds plaintext or passphrases, and what it does hold (ciphertext, size, access timestamps). #2060's trust constraint still forbids custodial keys.
3. **Unwrap throttling** — whether an OPRF-style blinded unwrap is adopted, which curve/construction, and how throttle state is keyed so it reveals nothing. If OPRF is rejected, record the cheaper alternative (e.g. per-identity attempt budget over the existing fixed-window limiter shape from #2333) with its guessing-cost analysis.
4. **Storage surface** — which hosted storage the blob lives in, retention, and deletion on key revocation.
5. **Restore-forces-rotation** — the flag's representation, which is #2380's keyset substrate.

## Acceptance
- [ ] A decision is recorded on this issue for items 1–5, or each is explicitly deferred with rationale.
- [ ] The server-never-sees-plaintext claim has a concrete protocol sketch (who computes what) that a reviewer can falsify.
- [ ] Follow-up implementation issues are filed from the decision, or the decision is to decline the server-side backup entirely.

## Out of scope
- Local envelope export/import (#2279), seed-phrase export/restore (#2381), guardian/social recovery (#2382), issuer key rotation (#2804).

## Sources
`doc/2026-10-29T11-28-18Z_investigation_key_recovery_hosted/` §4, §7, §11 slice 2; #2060 (closed); #2279; #2380; `pkgs/id/src/lib.rs:314`.


## Acceptance criteria

- A design is recorded settling: the backup blob format (AEAD + KDF versioned envelope, reusing #2279's header shape), the blinded-unwrap (OPRF-style) protocol, server-side rate limiting / throttling, and the server key-custody posture.
- The design names what the server learns and cannot learn (passphrase, key, blob contents) for each protocol step.
- An implementation issue is filed and linked as a native relation in the same pass the design lands (protocol §11 — a design with no implementation link is not finished work).

items.title: Rename sensitivity ladder identifiers in code to canonical public/internal/private/sensitive (aliases/migration, not a blind swap)

labels.name: stray-work
