items.body:
# Rename the sensitivity ladder identifiers in code to the canonical ladder (public < internal < private < sensitive)

## Why

The sensitivity ladder's canonical names were corrected on 2026-11-23. The classes are:

**`public < internal < private < sensitive`**

The old names are retired. They map onto the canonical rungs in order:

| Retired name (code today) | Canonical name |
|---|---|
| `shareable` | `public` |
| `personal` | `internal` |
| `local-only` | `private` |
| `secret-bearing` | `sensitive` |

Note: the retired `local-only` never meant "stored on the local laptop"; it was a rung name only.

## Scope of this issue: the CODE rename (not the prose sweep)

A companion prose sweep (living docs + the atlas/fleet/id books) is being done separately by Lane OA11 and will link its PR here. This issue owns the identifier rename in code, which must NOT be done as a blind search-and-replace, per the persisted-value caveat below.

## Code-surface inventory (measured 2026-11-23, `git grep -iE 'shareable|local-only|secret-bearing'` on main)

- `pkgs/atlas-search` (excluding its book): 33 files, ~379 lines. Includes the Rust `Sensitivity` enum (`Shareable / Personal / LocalOnly / SecretBearing`), the `SENS_ORDER` ordering in atlas-core, serde spellings, the `--max-sensitivity` CLI surface, service per-identity ceiling caps, disclosure-context ceilings, and the Worker/MCP pinned ceiling strings.
- `pkgs/id` (excluding its book): ~19 files, ~51 lines. (The id book's `local-only` occurrences are the ordinary English "runs only locally / not deployed" sense, not the ladder — not part of this rename.)
- `pkgs/fleet` (excluding its book): ~13 files, ~62 lines, including the `fleet search` `--max-sensitivity` pass-through and `docs/verbs.md`.
- `pkgs/mcpx`: ~6 code files, ~7 lines. (The mcpx book has zero ladder occurrences; its docs' `shareable`/`local-only` hits are ordinary prose and an upstream MCP spec identifier — not part of this rename.)
- Elsewhere: `pkgs/note-submission` (src + tests), `pm-stack/aggregator` (`server.ts`, `views.ts`, `views.test.ts`), `pkgs/gh-fleet/default.nix`, `nixos/home/atlas-backup.sh`, `nixos/home/laptop-repo-keeper.test.sh`.

## Persisted-serde caveat — stored values need alias/migration handling, never a blind swap

The retired strings are not just identifiers; they are stored and exchanged values:

- Scheme-1.0 `sensitivity` column labels in Atlas staging databases, and the published `chunks` / `session_labels` sensitivity labels in the corpus databases (at the frozen census: 100,060 `personal`, 6,941 `local-only`, 638 `secret-bearing` chunk labels).
- Per-identity ceiling configuration (e.g. the service's named client caps) and user config carrying ceiling values.
- CLI values: `--max-sensitivity` accepted spellings and its `personal` default, on `atlas-search`, `fleet search`, and related verbs; segment-file sensitivity names accepted by `atlas-stage`.
- Wire/JSON values: search envelope fields such as `max_sensitivity` and per-hit `sensitivity`, and the MCP tool description strings that quote the ceiling verbatim.

A rename therefore needs a compatibility design before any swap: serde aliases (accept old, emit new) or an explicit data migration for stored labels, a dual-accept window for CLI/config values, and a decided cutover for emitted JSON. Renaming the Rust enum variants and their serde spellings in one step would make existing databases, configs, and scripts unreadable.

## Open question — one ladder or two (decision still owed; do not decide inside the rename PR)

The docs currently present the corpus tiers (`public` / `internal` / `secret`) and the four-rung ceiling ladder as "two namings, one ladder" (see the atlas book glossary), with the working correspondence `shareable -> public`, `personal + local-only -> internal`, `secret-bearing -> secret`. After this rename, the ceiling ladder (`public < internal < private < sensitive`) will share the names `public` and `internal` with the tier vocabulary. Whether the end state is one unified ladder or two distinct vocabularies that happen to share two rung names is a deliberate decision that is still owed by the design owner. This issue records the question; the rename must not silently settle it.

## Acceptance shape (for whoever implements)

- [ ] Compatibility design recorded (aliases vs migration, per surface above).
- [ ] Code identifiers, enum variants, and CLI spellings renamed with the compatibility layer in place.
- [ ] Stored-label migration or alias-read verified against a copy of a staging + publish database.
- [ ] Books/reference updated to the new literal spellings in the same change (they currently document the legacy spellings as the code's values).

items.title: design: fleet transport & pooling — host selection without Tailscale, iroh for non-Muse agents, generic pool primitive
items.body:
## Direction

Drew, 2026-11-23 15:07 CST — the longer-term design threads that grow out of the laptop route codification (#13717, the route-form family; #13654 is its F1):

1. **Choosing hosts and access without Tailscale.**
2. **Direct iroh for non-Muse agents.**
3. **A generic pooling system.**

This issue tracks the design. The full design record lands as a dated doc (`doc/2026-11-23T21-10-36Z_design_fleet-transport-pooling/`); this issue carries the three threads as separable work items with the recommendation for each. Design only — every build item below needs its own slice issue when picked up.

## Premise check (read first, 2026-11-23)

- **#13717 already codifies the route forms** (3 methods × 2 shapes + the `fleet laptop` walker + the laptop-ssh F7 demotion). This design builds on it: thread 1 turns its laptop-specific matrix into per-host data; it does not redo it.
- **#10356 (2026-11-14) already designs explicit transport selection** — `fleet connect --method exec|ssh|job|auto`, sessions, drop semantics. Composition, not duplication: #10356 is *method choice on a known host*; thread 1 is *host choice + reach when no overlay exists*. #10356 also records the hard constraint: **the sandbox has no inbound path at all** — every connection is sandbox-initiated or rendezvoused. Any no-Tailscale design must name its rendezvous.
- **#2179 already specifies a machine registry as its target** ("a machine registry (identity, capabilities, …)") and a machine pool for placement. Thread 1 extends that registry with transport offers and identity bindings; it does not invent a second registry.
- **#1967 is closed with a recorded recommendation**: state the requirement (reach a daemon by cryptographic identity; NAT traversal with relay fallback; E2E + mutual auth from that identity), then pick the transport on merit — tsnet won *for mcpx, a Go binary*, because iroh is Rust and cgo/sidecar costs were priced in. Thread 2 does not reopen #1967: the fleet binary is Rust, so the embedding calculus that decided #1967 inverts for fleet-side components. For Go components #1967's answer stands.
- **opencode#2256 is closed** (fork PR #2598 landed the combined-signal wall). The live wall-scoping work is **#13693** (scope inference, alias providers, per-model free caps). Thread 3 aligns with #13693; it does not restart the wall debate.
- The fleet orchestration architecture record (`doc/2026-11-13T03-20-24Z_design_pm-stack-fleet-orchestration/architecture.md`) contains **no host-selection or transport design** (checked: no tailscale/iroh/placement material). The gap this design fills is real.

---

## Thread 1 — Host selection and access without Tailscale

**Problem.** Today "the laptop" is a hardcoded singleton, and two of its three route methods lean on the tailnet (laptop-agent legs hairpin the session proxy / DERP — #10356 measured warm ~0.4 s, cold CONNECT ~1.8 s; SSH rides a CONNECT proxy too). An agent with no tailnet — not enrolled, overlay down, or a non-Muse seat that never had one — has no route at all, even though the commander endpoint (#13404) already proves a non-Tailscale path: public HTTPS door (Cloudflare Worker gate) + tunnel to the host, OAuth/bearer auth, origin locked down.

**Shape.** A host is a registry record, not a name baked into scripts:

- **Static half** — the #2179 machine registry: host identity (one fleet identity per host, issued under the fleet CA program #9155 / the interim IdP CA), capabilities, and **transport offers**: for each transport the host serves — commander-style public door URL, laptop-agent endpoint, sshd, iroh NodeId — the offer carries its endpoint data and the credential *name* (never a value) that authenticates to it.
- **Live half** — the queue broker's seat records already track which seats are alive; the broker carries the live overlay (last-seen, load, health) on top of the static record. The broker is not the registry of record — it is a queue component, and its reachability is itself a bootstrap question.
- **Cold-start rendezvous** — DNS under our own zones publishes only the stable public doors (commander-style endpoints), so an agent with nothing but internet + DNS can find a first door. DNS carries offers, never secrets; liveness never comes from DNS.

**Selection.** Resolving a host yields candidate (host × transport-form) pairs — exactly the #13717 form matrix, as per-host data instead of a laptop table. Choosing among them is a pool decision (thread 3). `fleet laptop` is the N=1 special case of `fleet host <name>`.

**Access without Tailscale, per transport:**

| Transport | Reach without overlay | Auth at the door | Auth at the host |
|---|---|---|---|
| Commander-pattern public door (#13404) | Anywhere with internet | OAuth (agent/human identity) or machine bearer, by name from the secrets broker | The bridged service's own auth; origin lockdown (door is the only ingress) |
| iroh (thread 2) | Anywhere with internet; relay rendezvous, direct when punchable | NodeId allowlist (the key *is* the identity) | Application-layer authorization on top of the authenticated key (#1967's split: transport here, authorization separate) |
| Direct SSH/HTTP on public address | Only hosts with public reachability — not the general NAT case | sshd / daemon token | Same |
| Headscale (self-hosted tailnet control) | Removes the vendor, **not** the overlay — an agent with no overlay client still can't use it | Tailnet identity | Same as today's tailnet legs |

**Recommendation:** registry hybrid (static #2179 registry + broker live overlay + DNS cold-start doors), commander-pattern as the general no-overlay door, iroh as the peer-to-peer door (thread 2), Headscale recorded as "same shape, self-hosted" — not an answer to the no-overlay requirement. One host identity (fleet CA) binds all of a host's transport credentials, so adding a transport never mints a new identity.

**Work items (each its own slice when picked up):**
- 1a. Registry schema: extend #2179's record with transport offers + identity bindings (fleet cert, iroh NodeId, door URLs, credential names).
- 1b. Broker live overlay: last-seen/load/health keyed to the registry record.
- 1c. `fleet host` resolution + selection on top of the #13717 forms (the walker generalized from laptop to any host).
- 1d. DNS cold-start publication for public doors, with the offers-not-secrets rule written down.

## Thread 2 — Direct iroh for non-Muse agents

**Who this is for.** Fleet seats that are not Muse (opencode lanes, grok, felix, xaltha) ride routes built around Muse's session stack (session proxy, brokers, Muse enrollment). They deserve a transport that is theirs: direct, identity-addressed, no Muse session machinery in the path.

**What iroh is (from iroh's own docs, docs.rs `iroh` / `iroh-net`):**

- **Addressing/identity.** Every node has an ed25519 keypair; the public key is the **NodeId** and is the node's stable identity. QUIC's TLS handshake uses the node's secret key — there is no certificate chain; connecting to a NodeId *is* authenticating that node, and an accepting node learns the peer's authenticated NodeId. Authorization (which NodeIds may do what) is the application's job — an allowlist at accept time, per-ALPN protocol.
- **Connection shape.** A connection usually starts through the node's **home relay**, then upgrades to a direct path via hole punching (QUIC-native traversal in the current line); if no direct path exists, the relay path simply carries the connection. Relays forward **encrypted traffic addressed by NodeId only** — a relay cannot read payloads.
- **Discovery is composable** (the `Discovery` trait; multiple services run concurrently): DNS discovery backed by **pkarr** — signed DNS packets (key = NodeId) published via a pkarr relay and served by an `iroh-dns-server` (n0 runs a public instance; both server pieces are self-hostable); a pkarr resolver over HTTP; DHT discovery over the BitTorrent Mainline; and local-network (mDNS-style) swarm discovery. **Tickets** bundle NodeId + relay URL + direct addresses for out-of-band bootstrap with no lookup service at all.
- **Relay dependence, honestly:** a relay (or known direct addresses) is required to *start* most connections; it is a rendezvous + fallback, not a middleman for established direct traffic. Depending on n0's public relays is optional — `iroh-relay` is self-hostable with ACME TLS, per-client rate limits, and metrics.
- **Embedding.** iroh is a Rust crate (`Endpoint` builder, ALPN-based protocol router). In a Rust binary it is a library dependency — no FFI, no sidecar, no second process. (For Go, #1967's pricing stands: `iroh-ffi` via cgo, or a sidecar. A third-party Go port exists — unverified maturity; do not plan on it.)

**Replaces vs complements:**

- *Replaces*, for non-Muse seats: the rendezvous + traversal role the session proxy / DERP hairpin plays today, and the Cloudflare tunnel for point-to-point host traffic.
- *Complements*: the commander public door stays — hosted MCP clients (ChatGPT/Claude connectors) cannot run iroh and need an HTTPS door. tsnet stays where it already works (mcpx's Go daemon per #1967; the Muse session stack is untouched by this thread).

**Recommendation:** pilot iroh as one transport offer in the thread-1 registry for **one** non-Muse seat class — opencode-lane host reach (seat ↔ laptop without the session-proxy hairpin) — with the fleet binary (Rust) hosting the endpoint. Self-host one `iroh-relay` + pkarr/DNS under our own zones (n0's public relays only as bootstrap fallback), publish host NodeIds in the registry (1a), allowlist by NodeId bound to fleet identities. Measure against #10356's numbers: direct-path rate, p50/p99 setup + call latency vs the ~0.4 s warm hairpin. Pin the iroh version and hide it behind fleet's own transport trait — the crate is young and its API has moved before (iroh-net → iroh renames).

**Work items:**
- 2a. Pilot: fleet binary endpoint + one seat class; direct-path/latency record against the hairpin baseline.
- 2b. Self-hosted relay + pkarr/DNS under our zones; NodeId ↔ fleet identity binding in the registry.
- 2c. Accept-side allowlist + per-ALPN authorization shape (composes with the fleet CA / #9155 identity work).

## Thread 3 — A generic pooling system

**Problem.** The estate keeps reinventing the same machine: model pools (route tables, wall doctrine, failover — #13693, opencode#2256), the google-free round-robin (four projects, per-model-per-project caps), the route-form walker (#13717: ordered attempts, advance only on failure-to-serve, name the serving form), fleet placement (#2179 machine pool; #13611: unread load reads as *unknown*, never zero), and now host×transport selection (thread 1). Each re-implementation re-learns the same lessons — usually by hitting the same wall twice.

**The primitive owns** (domain-independent):

- **Member state machine** — serving / demoted / walled / probing, per member, with the wall keyed at the **narrowest true scope** the evidence supports (member, group, provider, account — the scope is data, with widening/narrowing rules: a sibling's success narrows a wide wall; repeated member failures at a shared scope widen it). This is #13693's doctrine stated once, generically.
- **Attempt semantics** — the #13717 distinction, generalized: advance to the next member on *failure to serve*; a served failure (the member answered and the answer was no) is recorded, classified, and only advances per the classifier's verdict.
- **Selection strategies as plug-ins** — ordered (tier walk), round-robin (google-free), weighted (route tables), free-first (an ordering by cost class), least-loaded where a load read exists — with #13611's rule built in: **an unread load is unknown, and unknown never sorts as zero**.
- **Recovery** — wall expiry at a recorded reset, probe-based re-admission (a bounded successful probe re-seats a member), and measured-increase rejoin (opencode#2256's path). One failed call never benches forever; a wall without a reset still gates (bounded inferred walls, per #13693 slice P / PR #13735).
- **Observability** — every selection decision records member, state, and reason. The form-visibility rule from #13717, generalized: a pool decision you cannot read back is a bug.

**The domain keeps** (not the primitive's business):

- What a member *is*: a model leg, a (host × transport-form) pair, a machine, a compile slot.
- Measurement: quota gatherers, latency probes, Actions-load reads — and the **classifiers** that turn a failure into a class (quota / transport / auth / served-refusal). The primitive consumes classified outcomes; it does not classify.
- Policy: weights, free-first ordering, reserve rules (OpenAI last), pace guards (#2732).

**Options:**
- (a) **A shared Rust crate in the fleet workspace** (working name `fleet-pool`): `Member` / `Classifier` / `Strategy` / `Probe` traits + the state machine. First consumers: the route-form walker (smallest, already specified in #13717) and host×transport selection (thread 1). Model routes consume it at the proxy/fork boundary through a recorded-outcome interface only — **not** a rewrite of #13693's in-flight work. Placement adopts last; its fairness/lease semantics (cf. id spill, #7572) stay domain-side.
- (b) Spec-only pattern, each domain re-implements: zero migration cost, and exactly the drift that produced this thread.
- (c) One central pool service: a single decision point — right for the compile coordinator's atomic cross-owner claims (a separate, already-directed build), wrong as the general shape: it makes every route decision a network hop and a shared failure point.

**Recommendation:** (a), adopted in the order walker → host×transport → model-route boundary → placement, each adoption its own slice with the domain's existing tests as the oracle.

**Work items:**
- 3a. `fleet-pool` crate: state machine + strategies + decision log, property-tested (wall scope invariants named as oracles).
- 3b. Walker adoption (#13717 composition becomes the crate's first consumer).
- 3c. Model-route boundary interface (recorded outcomes in, selection out) — sequenced after #13693 lands its scoping layer.
- 3d. Placement adoption review against #2179 (may legitimately conclude "not yet").

## Cross-links

#13654 (commander subcommand, form F1) · #13717 (route-form family) · #10356 (fleet connect: method selection, sessions) · #2179 (machine pool + registry) · #1967 (iroh and the Go-binding question — closed, recommendation stands for Go) · #13669 (mcpx→Rust pilot; tsnet is Go-only, iroh the Rust-side option) · #13693 (wall scoping) · opencode#2256 (wall doctrine — closed) · #13404 (commander endpoint, the non-Tailscale proof) · #9155 (fleet CA — the identity layer hosts bind to) · #8991 / #9399 (pool routing epics — thread 3 serves these, does not replace them)

items.body:
## Direction (Drew, 2026-10-31)

Atlas moves from a single canonical DB + one Turso publish to provenance-first, scalable infrastructure. Design doc: hatch-personal `workspace/turso-atlas/docs/atlas-provenance-and-scale-design-2026-10-31.md`.

Rules:
1. Keep ALL data — nothing stripped from atlas.db or publishes to save space; only byte-identical dupes are cleaned, backups kept.
2. Backups AND plain extracts for every corpus.
3. Every chunk records EVERY place it was found: `chunk_occurrences` (chunk → array of source locators with spans, observed_at). Today dedup silently drops occurrences (~127K at first ingest); 6,344 canonical sessions own zero chunks for exactly this reason and their occurrences are unrecorded.
4. Every import is interned content-addressed (laptop extracts CAS / R2, registry maps CA hash → normal paths) or pinned as `repo@commit:path`. Registry also holds line numbers / dates / spans for extracts.
5. Retrieval: vector/FTS search across multiple Turso shard DBs (collection × month) returns IDs; a catalog/registry resolves an ID to a file, a chunk, or a start–end section — including a member of a tar in R2 (sidecar index, range fetch) or a local file.

Verified state feeding this (2026-10-31): canonical 18,325 sessions / 122,124 messages / 107,639 chunks; local-only = 6,941 chunks of personal-client TEXT held back from Turso by policy (not missing embeddings); Turso atlas 1.0 GB / 100,698 chunks; laptop ~/atlas 12 GB contains NO consequential byte-identical duplicates (hash-verified) — it is distinct versions/working sets, so no cleanup windfall exists.

## Phases
1. Add `chunk_occurrences` + `cas_registry` to canonical atlas.db; ingest writes occurrences from now on (no re-embed, no republish).
2. Laptop extracts dir + CAS; atlas-backup covers it; backfill extracts for sources still on disk.
3. Occurrence backfill from CAS extracts; document the local-only publish predicate in the publish script.
4. Catalog DB + shard layout at next publish growth (or full message-archive ingest); resolution as MCP tools (search → ids → resolve → fetch span).

<!-- agent-note:v1 agent=muse state=filed source=main-chat-2026-10-31 -->

## Acceptance criteria

- A `chunk_occurrences` provenance registry exists: every chunk records every source locator it was found at (with spans and observed_at), including occurrences previously dropped by dedup.
- Backups AND plain extracts exist for every corpus; imports are interned content-addressed (CAS hash → path registry) or pinned as `repo@commit:path`, with line numbers / dates / spans recorded for extracts.
- Retrieval works across multiple Turso shard DBs (collection × month): vector/FTS search returns IDs and the catalog/registry resolves an ID to a file, chunk, or start–end section (including a tar member in R2 via sidecar index + range fetch, or a local file).
- No data is stripped to save space; only byte-identical duplicates are cleaned, with backups kept.

items.body:
# fleet queue: resume-by-session, claim-any-task, and manual-only items

**Priority: High. Intrinsic urgency: 400.** Drew directive, 2026-11-12 20:41 CST.

Parent epic: #8990 (fleet tool — one door for coordination, mirroring, and backups).

## Why this exists

The Fleet CA design mill incident exposed a queue-semantics gap. Epic #9155's bound Summit session was stopped and queue task 15345 was parked. The eventual resume had to create a fresh OpenCode session and rebuild the design context from artifacts; roughly 600K tokens of shared context from the stopped Summit run were not recoverable through the queue because a task cannot name the session that should resume it.

The queue needs first-class support for four related operations:

1. resume a task in a named OpenCode session;
2. claim any specific task by number, including a parked or attempt-capped task, under an explicit owner override;
3. claim several tasks under one session; and
4. create work that automatic lanes never claim.

Section 5 records a broader fleet-attribution proposal for an explicit decision. It is **not** adopted by filing this issue.

## 1. Resume by session ID

### Specification

- Add a nullable `resume_session_id` column to the fleet-queue `tasks` table. It may be set when a task is enqueued or by an authorized later update.
- When a worker claims a task with `resume_session_id`, the launcher must continue that OpenCode session by session ID instead of creating a new session. This builds on the session-state work in #9075 and the create-path provenance stamping in #9073.
- Record both the requested session and the session actually used on the task's claim/attempt record. A silent substitution is not allowed.
- Only an authorized actor may set, replace, or clear the value: the task creator, the currently bound worker/session, or an explicit operator action. Every change is audit-logged with actor, prior value, new value, time, and reason.
- The resume hint does not override task ownership. If the task is already claimed, section 3's normal skip/take-over rules apply.

### Edge cases to settle in the design and cover with tests

- **Session no longer exists on the target OpenCode server:** fall back to a fresh session in the correct worktree, record `resume_fallback=missing_session` and the new session ID on the task, and surface the substitution in the claim result. Do not fail forever or repeatedly retry the missing session.
- **Session exists in a different worktree:** never silently execute the task in the wrong tree. Either (a) require an explicit rebind action that records old worktree, new worktree, actor, and reason, or (b) fall back to a fresh session in the task's worktree and record the mismatch. The implementation issue must choose one rule and test it; silent cross-worktree execution is prohibited.
- **Session exists but is busy/owned by another active task:** do not steal it implicitly. The claim is skipped unless the section 3 take-over path is explicitly used.
- **Host/server restart:** the stored session ID survives in the queue. On claim, existence is checked against the target server; the missing-session fallback above applies if the server no longer knows it.
- **No `resume_session_id`:** behavior is unchanged from today.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Schema migration adds `resume_session_id` and the audit fields/events needed to distinguish requested session from actual session.
- [ ] Enqueue and update paths can set/clear the column with authorization checks and audit records.
- [ ] A claim with a live matching session continues that session; evidence from the OpenCode server shows the same session ID receiving the task prompt.
- [ ] Missing-session, wrong-worktree, and busy-session cases each have automated tests and produce the specified recorded outcome.
- [ ] A task without `resume_session_id` follows the existing claim path unchanged.

## 2. Claim any task by number, including parked or attempt-capped tasks

### Specification

- Provide a fleet CLI verb for claiming one task by numeric ID. Working name: `fleet queue claim --task <id>`. The final verb must follow the existing fleet queue verb conventions from #9016.
- The claim path must be able to claim a task that is queued, parked, or at `max_attempts`. It must not pretend those states do not exist; it records an explicit **manual-claim override**.
- The override record includes claimant identity, session ID when known, timestamp, reason, prior task status, prior `not_before`/park reason when present, and prior attempt count.
- A manual claim does **not** silently reset the attempt history. The max-attempts gate is bypassed for this claim by the recorded override, while the historical attempts remain visible.
- The resulting claim carries an override marker/epoch that startup and supervision logic can see. A worker booting under that manual claim must not immediately re-stop or re-park the task for the same unchanged condition that caused the earlier park. A materially new condition may still stop or park it, with that new condition recorded.
- Repeating the same claim while the same worker/session owns it is idempotent and returns the existing claim. A claim by a different worker follows section 3's skip/take-over rules.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A specific queued task can be claimed by ID without waiting for normal lane selection.
- [ ] A specific parked task can be claimed by ID; the resulting task record shows the override, prior park state, actor, session, time, and reason.
- [ ] A specific task at `max_attempts` can be claimed by ID without erasing attempt history.
- [ ] A manually claimed task's first boot does not re-park solely for the same recorded park condition; a test reproduces the original park condition and proves the override is honored.
- [ ] A second claim by the same owner is idempotent; an attempted claim by another owner does not disturb the live claim unless take-over is explicitly requested.

## 3. Claim multiple tasks under one session

### Specification

- Extend the claim verb so one session can claim multiple task IDs in one operation, for example `fleet queue claim --task <id1> --task <id2> --session <session-id>`.
- The result is reported per task: `claimed`, `already-owned-by-this-session`, `skipped-claimed`, `not-found`, or `failed`, with the reason for each non-claim.
- Tasks already picked up by another worker are skipped by default.
- An explicit `--take-over` flag may claim an already-picked-up task. A take-over atomically transfers the lease/claim, ends or supersedes the prior claim according to the queue's lease rules, and records prior worker/session, new worker/session, actor, time, and reason. Where the prior worker can be signalled, it receives a hand-back/stop signal; where it cannot, that limitation is recorded.
- Resume-by-session, parked, max-attempts, and manual-only semantics compose with batch claims: each task's override/take-over/manual authorization is independently auditable.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] One command can claim at least two unclaimed tasks for the same session and returns a per-task result.
- [ ] Already-claimed tasks are skipped by default and their existing claims are unchanged.
- [ ] With `--take-over`, an already-claimed task transfers to the requesting session and both sides of the transfer are audit-logged.
- [ ] A mixed batch (unclaimed, already owned by requester, owned by another worker, missing, parked) produces the specified per-task outcomes without disturbing skipped tasks.

## 4. Manual-only queue items

Automatic lanes must have a trustworthy way to leave an item alone until a person or a named session claims it. Direct-dispatch design-mill work is the immediate use case: today such work is made effectively manual by parking it or by relying on dispatch discipline, but neither state says what it means.

### Options

| Option | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Create the item as parked, then manually claim/start it | Works as a stopgap and needs no schema, but conflates “waiting for a stated condition/date” with “waiting for a human/named session.” It also inherits park semantics, including watchers and reports treating the item as stalled or blocked. |
| Give it a very, very low priority | Not a guarantee. Priority changes, queue drains, priority boosts, and lane scope changes can all make the item claimable. It is a race, not a contract. |
| **First-class `manual_only` / `no_auto_claim` flag (recommended)** | States the actual contract. The automatic claim query excludes the item regardless of priority. Only the explicit claim-by-ID path can claim it. The flag and every change to it are auditable. |

### Recommendation and specification

Adopt a first-class boolean, working name `manual_only`, on `tasks`:

- The automatic claim query must exclude `manual_only = true` unconditionally; priority, age, lane, and queue depth do not change that.
- The item remains visible in queue listings and dashboards with its manual-only state shown as an intentional state, not as parked, stalled, or blocked.
- Only section 2's explicit claim-by-ID path can claim it. Batch claims follow the same rule per task.
- The flag may be set at enqueue time or by an authorized later update. Setting or clearing it is audit-logged. Clearing it makes the item eligible for normal automatic claiming.
- Migration: audit current parked-for-manual/direct-dispatch items individually and convert only those whose record shows they are waiting for a human/named session. Do not blanket-convert parked tasks; most parks mean something else.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Schema and enqueue/update paths support `manual_only` with audit history.
- [ ] With a manual-only item as the highest-priority and only otherwise-claimable item, an automatic lane run claims nothing.
- [ ] The same item can be claimed through the explicit claim-by-ID path, including under a named session.
- [ ] Queue listings distinguish manual-only from parked and blocked.
- [ ] A migration report lists current parked-for-manual candidates and the disposition of each; no blanket conversion occurs.

## 5. Proposal for decision — fleet init, run identity, and a complete transaction log

**Status: proposal to decide, not an approved design.** Drew's suggestion, recorded here so the decision is explicit:

> Use the fleet tool for queue and GitHub interactions. Require a fleet init step that mints a unique run/task ID and stamps everything discoverable — or require a flag/env var that ties that ID to a task or cron job. Carry the ID into GitHub operations so comments, edits, closes, and merges are attributable to the run that performed them. Log every fleet transaction to a durable log file that is backed up and can be injected into Atlas.

The motivation is concrete: the automation that labeled #9155 `status:done` and closed it during an active bound Summit run has not been identified from the GitHub surface alone. A fleet-carried run identity and transaction log would make “who stopped, merged, closed, or edited this?” a lookup instead of an investigation.

### Decisions this issue must produce

- [ ] **Scope:** Does “all interactions” mean all fleet-mediated queue/GitHub mutations, all GitHub operations including reads, interactive human use as well as agents/cron, or a phased scope? Which bypasses remain allowed, and how are they detected?
- [ ] **Init contract:** What does `fleet init` mint and stamp (run ID, task ID, cron/job ID, session ID, host, worktree, repo, actor/route, start time)? What is inherited from env, the #9075 pwd-file, flags, and task claims? What happens when init is missing: fail closed for mutations, warn-and-log, or read-only mode? Is there an audited emergency bypass?
- [ ] **GitHub carriage:** How is the run ID represented on issue/PR comments, edits, closes, and merges — pm-metadata, a hidden marker, a database mapping, or a combination — without noisy duplication on every operation?
- [ ] **Transaction log:** Append-only local file, queue/DB table, or both? Required fields, secret-redaction rules, rotation/retention, backup target/frequency, failure behavior when logging fails, and the Atlas ingestion path/schema.
- [ ] **Adoption boundary:** If adopted, file separate implementation issues for init/identity, GitHub carriage, and logging/backup/Atlas ingestion. If rejected or narrowed, record the rationale and the alternative attribution mechanism.

### Acceptance criteria for this section

- [ ] A decision record exists for the proposal (see the companion decision-records issue) stating adopted, narrowed, or rejected, with scope and rationale.
- [ ] No implementation of fleet-init is treated as authorized merely because the proposal appears in this issue.
- [ ] If adopted, follow-on implementation issues are filed and linked here before work begins.

## Cross-links

- Incident and motivating case: #9155 (queue task 15345; stopped bound Summit, parked task, fresh-session resume).
- Session state in env + worktree pwd-file: #9075.
- Fleet create-path Metadata/provenance stamping: #9073.
- Higher-level fleet GitHub tools on token rotation: #9016.
- Parent epic: #8990.

## Overall acceptance

- [ ] Sections 1–4 are implemented with migrations, CLI help/docs, audit records, and the tests named above.
- [ ] Existing tasks without a resume session or manual-only flag behave exactly as before.
- [ ] Queue docs/runbooks describe resume, manual claim, take-over, and manual-only semantics using the same terms as the CLI and task records.
- [ ] Section 5 ends in an explicit decision record, not silent adoption or silent abandonment.

items.body:
## Long-term tracker: migrate the pm stack into Supabase and refactor its parts into schemas for central management

Drew asked for this as the long-term tracking issue (2026-10-31). The pm stack (aggregator, fleet feed, dashboard, orchestration, dispatch, usage hub) grew up as local files and laptop-local stores. The direction, proven piece by piece on 2026-10-31, is: state lives in Supabase (muse-dev2) in domain-appropriate schemas, components read/write the database, and local files become caches or exports — never the only copy.

### Where things stand (verified 2026-10-31)
Already Supabase-backed:
- Repo-queue backend (recovered onto muse-dev2 in the 2026-10-30 cutover; see #2767/#2768).
- Session mirror (agent schema mirror tables).
- Usage snapshots / usage hub collectors (#1050, #1111).
- Domain event streams: ainventory, engineering, finance, research, automation, home — tasks append typed events; orchestration-pass began appending material changes to automation.events on 2026-10-31.

Still local-only:
- Orchestrator working state: orchestration.json / orchestrator-state.json / orchestrator-log.md (goal workspace hidden_files) — the dashboard reads these files.
- Aggregator actions store + comments store (laptop-local) — Drew's dashboard triage actions and comments.
- Fleet-feed JSON pipeline (collector -> scp -> laptop aggregator serving JSON files).
- Backlog markdown files the orchestrator reads (backlog-*.md in the goal workspace).

### Scope (phased, each phase its own implementation issue)
1. Orchestration state: move tier/classification state + run log to Supabase tables (automation schema or a dedicated pm schema); orchestration.json becomes a generated export for the dashboard contract (#898 shape preserved).
2. Aggregator stores: actions + comments into Supabase with the same apply/result semantics (#1152/#1154/#1156 contracts preserved); the laptop aggregator reads/writes the DB.
3. Feed pipeline: fleet-feed snapshots land as DB rows first; the served JSON is derived, not transported.
4. Backlogs/queues: backlog state derived from DB + GitHub instead of hand-maintained markdown (markdown becomes a view).
5. Central management: one schema map (pm-stack/SHARED-SCHEMA-MAP.md, with the migration plan at pm-stack/SHARED-SCHEMA-MIGRATION-PLAN.md), one place to inspect/pause/repair every component's state.

### Non-goals / constraints
- No big-bang rewrite: each phase keeps the current file-based path working until the DB path is verified, then flips.
- Dashboard contracts (#898 orchestration shape, actions/comments semantics) do not change shape — only their backing store.
- Single-writer rules stay: orchestrator is the only writer to the GitHub Project; the same discipline applies per table.
- Secrets by name only; muse-dev2 is canonical (old muse-dev is dead; pointer audit tracked in #2796).

Related: #2767, #2768, #2796, #898, #899, #910, #2155.

### Phase implementation issues (filed 2026-11-03, task 8438):
- Phase 1 (orchestration state): #5005
- Phase 2 (aggregator stores / shared tables): #1744 (pilot area #941)
- Phase 3 (feed pipeline DB-first): #5006
- Phase 4 (backlogs as a view): #5007
- Phase 5 (central management surface): #5008

items.title: id: implement server-side identity backup per #5033 decision (v1 envelope blob, epoch-guarded storage, download budget)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/l
labels.description: Large: multi-day or open-ended; expect staged check-ins

items.body:
## Problem
Issue #5033 recorded the design decision (2026-11-08, task 12716) for a server-side identity backup: the blob is the #2279 v1 envelope byte-for-byte, the server holds ciphertext + metadata only, OPRF is rejected for v1 in favour of a per-identity download budget over the pkgs/id/src/abuse.rs limiter shape plus the Argon2id guessing-cost floor, storage is one epoch-guarded record per identity with signed deletion, and restore-forces-rotation is deferred to the #2380 keyset substrate with an interim restore_epoch + device-notification rule. Nothing of this exists in code: at main 9f5a92057d pkgs/id has no backup record, endpoint, or lifecycle, and the identity key is still the raw file at pkgs/id/src/lib.rs:324.

## Implementation scope (from the #5033 decision)
- Server backup record keyed by hex(SHA-256(identity public key)) holding only: envelope bytes, envelope SHA-256, blob size, upload/download timestamps, monotone upload epoch, throttle counters, restore_epoch, and a deletion tombstone (H(pub) + final epoch).
- Upload endpoint: accepts envelope bytes + Sign_identity(H(pub) || envelope_sha256 || epoch); verifies the signature against the named public key; rejects non-increasing epochs; overwrites only on a valid higher-epoch upload.
- Download endpoint: requester presents the identity public key; server enforces the download budget (10/hour, 50/day per H(pub), weighted fixed windows per pkgs/id/src/abuse.rs, plus existing per-IP/global limits, refusals with retry-after) and returns the envelope bytes. Decryption stays client-side via the existing pkgs/id/src/key_envelope.rs import path; the passphrase never leaves the device.
- Delete endpoint: signed by the identity key; deletes ciphertext + counters, leaves the tombstone; account deletion purges the tombstone.
- Restore bookkeeping: a download-for-restore increments restore_epoch and notifies bound devices before the restored key is treated as authoritative for new group epochs (interim rule from #5033 item 5). Do NOT implement a rotation flag: that representation belongs to #2380 and lands there.
- Client: backup create/upload flow reusing key_envelope.rs encryption exactly (no second format), with a weak-passphrase warning at creation (per #5033 item 3's guessing-cost analysis).

## Acceptance
- [ ] A server data dump for a backup record contains no field beyond the #5033 item-2 list (test asserts the stored field set).
- [ ] Upload with a bad signature or a stale/equal epoch is rejected; a higher-epoch signed upload replaces the blob (tests naming their oracle: the #5033 decision items 1 and 4).
- [ ] The 11th download within an hour and the 51st within a day for one H(pub) are refused with retry-after (property test over the limiter: the budget invariant holds for arbitrary interleavings).
- [ ] Restore flow recovers the identity key from passphrase + downloaded envelope using only the existing key_envelope.rs decrypt path; wrong passphrase fails locally with no server signal.
- [ ] Signed delete removes the ciphertext; replaying the pre-delete signed upload does not resurrect it.
- [ ] No rotation flag is introduced; restore_epoch increment + bound-device notification are covered by tests.

## Out of scope
OPRF/blinded unwrap (rejected for v1 on #5033, revisit only as a v2 online assist), seed-phrase restore (#2381), guardian recovery (#2382), the restore-forces-rotation flag representation (#2380).

## Sources
Design decision on #5033 (comment 6718342769); investigation doc/2026-10-29T11-28-18Z_investigation_key_recovery_hosted sections 4.2, 7, 8.4; pkgs/id/src/key_envelope.rs; pkgs/id/src/abuse.rs.

## Acceptance criteria
- The v1 backup envelope format is documented in the implementation: version field, epoch semantics, and blob layout, matching the #5033 decision items 1-4.
- A server-side identity backup can be written and restored round-trip in tests, with epoch mismatch and malformed-blob cases refused with named errors.
- No client key material is logged or persisted outside the envelope; restore requires the documented epoch/credential checks.
- Tests named per the testing doctrine (invariant/oracle stated) cover round-trip, epoch roll, and corruption cases.

items.body:
## Problem

Agents open PRs and leave them. On 2026-11-22 the repository has 20 ready (non-draft) PRs opened by fleet agents and not merged. 12 have no unresolved review finding; 8 have findings nobody answered. The oldest is from 2026-11-19.

The job that used to finish these is `stale-pr-warden` (`doc/fleet-schedule-registry.md`: daily at 10:12, goal `keep-the-four-repos-healthy`). It files a `pr_shepherd` task per merge-ready PR. The last `pr_shepherd` tasks in the queue store are 17533 to 17535 (2026-11-16) and 20702 (2026-11-17). None since, while the registry still lists the job as enabled.

A task that produces a PR completes when the PR exists. Nothing then owns the review findings or the merge, so the issue stays open, its waiters stay blocked, and the branch drifts until it conflicts.

| PR | Opened | Unanswered findings | Title |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| #11979 | 11-19 | yes | docs: publish first C5 efficiency report |
| #12008 | 11-19 | no | fix(fleet): refresh lock for atlas blake3 dependency |

items.body:
## Summary

Expand #2046 (serverless edition — `id` on Cloudflare Workers) with the storage decision it left open: what is the backing store for `id` when it runs on Workers, and can the answer be more than one store?

This is a design investigation, not an implementation ticket. Its deliverable is a decision-ready comparison of **Cloudflare D1 vs Turso (libSQL) vs offering both**, a recommendation with the conditions that would flip it, and follow-on design tickets (see Decomposition sketch) detailed enough to be broken into implementation work without re-litigating the choice.

Relates to: #2046 (serverless edition on Cloudflare Workers), #806 (F12.13 journal replication — read replicas over a signed stream).

## Why this matters

The serverless edition promises `id` with no server to run. That promise lives or dies on the store underneath it:

- Every `id` invariant — identity, capability grants, journal / event history, world state — has to survive on a store whose consistency, replication, and failure model were designed for edge web apps, not necessarily for a signed, replicated journal.
- Picking the wrong store does not just cost performance; it can silently weaken the journal's guarantees (ordering, durability, replay) or lock the serverless edition into a cost / limits shape that only appears at scale.
- Conversely, supporting two stores doubles the storage-abstraction surface forever. "Both" must be justified, bounded, and priced — not adopted as an avoidance of deciding.

## Options to compare

### A. D1 only

- Native to Cloudflare: Workers binding, no extra vendor, no extra credentials for the operator.
- SQLite semantics; single-primary with read replication where available. Evaluate consistency model in detail: write consistency, read-your-writes within a session, replica lag, and what happens across regions.
- Fit for the `id` journal (#806): can the signed journal be stored, ordered, and replicated with the guarantees #806 assumes? Where does D1 replication help, and where does the signed stream have to do its own work regardless?
- Limits: database size, row / query limits, Time Travel / point-in-time recovery, backup / export story for an operator who wants to leave Cloudflare.

### B. Turso (libSQL) only

- libSQL as a SQLite fork with replication as a first-class feature (embedded replicas, primary replication). Evaluate the same consistency questions as D1, plus embedded-replica sync latency and offline behaviour.
- Fit for #806: does libSQL replication compose with — or conflict with — replication over a signed stream? Two replication systems moving the same data is a hazard to name explicitly.
- Operational shape: an external dependency and account even in the "serverless" edition; self-hosted sqld as an escape hatch; what that does to the "just deploy to Workers" story.
- Cost and limits at hobby, small-community, and large-world scales.

### C. Both — per-world or per-deployment choice

- A storage-backend abstraction with D1 and Turso as interchangeable implementations, chosen per deployment, or finer: per world.
- Price the abstraction honestly: which `id` storage operations must be in the common subset, what backend-specific features are then forbidden, how migrations between backends work (export journal → replay into the other store?), and how tests / CI cover two backends without doubling flakiness.
- Per-world choice adds a routing / metadata question: where is the "which store holds this world" fact itself stored, and what happens when a world's store is unreachable?
- State the decision rule for when "both" is worth it (e.g. operator sovereignty, an existing Turso estate, D1 limits hit in practice) vs when it is speculative generality.

## Comparison axes (required in the deliverable)

For each option, address every axis — "unknown, needs spike" is an acceptable entry, an omitted axis is not:

1. **Consistency & ordering** — write consistency, cross-region behaviour, session guarantees, ordering available to the journal.
2. **Replication / journal fit (#806)** — how store replication interacts with signed-stream replication; single-writer assumptions; conflict and fork behaviour.
3. **Cost shape** — free / entry tier, per-read / per-write / per-row pricing, storage pricing, egress; modelled at three scales (single user, small community, large public world). Include the cost of the Workers tier needed in each case.
4. **Limits & ceilings** — DB size, request / query limits, connection model from Workers, cold-start and latency profile by region.
5. **Local-dev story** — local D1 (Wrangler / Miniflare) vs local libSQL / sqld; can a developer run the full serverless edition offline? Seed / fixture / reset ergonomics; parity between local and deployed behaviour and known divergences.
6. **Durability, backup & exit** — backup, point-in-time recovery, export in an open format, migration off the platform; data-loss windows.
7. **Security & tenancy** — credentials / bindings, per-world isolation, row-level isolation assumptions, encryption-at-rest story, what a compromised Worker can reach.
8. **Operational burden** — what the operator must provision, monitor, and pay for; failure modes visible to end users.

## Non-goals

- Implementing either backend (this issue decides and decomposes; implementation is follow-on work).
- Re-designing the journal itself (#806 owns the signed-stream design); this issue only evaluates store fit against it.
- Non-serverless storage (self-hosted edition storage is out of scope except where the abstraction in option C would leak into it — flag any such leak explicitly).
- Choosing other serverless platforms (Workers is the #2046 premise).

## Acceptance criteria for the design deliverable

- [ ] A comparison document covering options A / B / C across all eight axes above, linked from this issue.
- [ ] A stated recommendation, the evidence behind it, and the conditions that would reverse it.
- [ ] An explicit statement of which journal guarantees (#806) each store preserves, weakens, or requires compensating design for.
- [ ] If "both" is recommended: the common storage contract, the choice granularity (per-deployment vs per-world), and the migration path between backends.
- [ ] Cost model at the three named scales, with assumptions listed.
- [ ] Follow-on design tickets filed from the Decomposition sketch (or the sketch revised with reasons).

## Decomposition sketch

Follow-on design tickets to be filed from this issue (indicative; revise during the work):

1. Design: storage contract for the serverless edition — the minimal `id` storage interface both backends must satisfy (journal append/read, world state, indexes).
2. Design / spike: D1 journal fit — ordering, sessions, and replication behaviour against the #806 signed-stream requirements, with a small proof of concept.
3. Design / spike: Turso / libSQL journal fit — embedded replicas and primary replication composed with #806, with a small proof of concept.
4. Design: local-dev parity for the serverless edition — Wrangler/Miniflare vs local sqld, fixtures, and the offline developer workflow.
5. Design: backend choice & migration — per-deployment vs per-world selection, where the routing fact lives, and export/replay migration between D1 and Turso.
6. Design: cost & limits guardrails — quotas, backpressure, and operator-visible warnings when a world approaches D1 / Turso ceilings.
7. Design: backup, recovery & exit for serverless storage — point-in-time recovery, open-format export, and leaving Cloudflare / Turso.

## Open questions

- Does #806's signed stream actually need store-level replication at all, or is store replication redundant (or actively harmful) once the journal replicates itself?
- Is per-world backend choice a real operator need, or is per-deployment enough? What evidence would distinguish the two?
- What is the largest world (events, state size, write rate) the serverless edition intends to support — and does either store's ceiling rule it out before cost does?
- How much D1 / Turso behaviour can only be learned from a running spike vs vendor documentation, and which claims in the comparison are documentation-only?
- If both are supported, who owns keeping the second backend honest — CI matrix, contract tests, or manual verification per release?
- Does Turso's self-hosted sqld option blur the line between the serverless and self-hosted editions in a useful way, or create a third, accidental edition?

# Provider self-renewal audit — 2026-11-09

Drew's rule (2026-11-09 20:42 CST): **all the providers renew themselves.** Every OAuth/token credential must refresh itself automatically; a provider dying on an expired token because renewal was missing, mis-targeted, or unprovisioned is a defect. Tonight produced three instances of that defect class — openai.main (sync wrote to the wrong door; fixed, fork PR #2237), _claude (credential blanked Nov 7; restored by hand), _antigravity (client secret never provisioned; fixed, PRs #8098/#8099). This audit checks **every** door against the rule so the class is closed, not just tonight's three instances.

Method (all reads 2026-11-10 ~02:45–03:00Z, laptop, generation 551, fork build ff9858a = deployed HEAD): live config pair `opencode.jsonc` (17 providers), credential store (24 rows, metadata only — no values read), deployed source (`packages/core/src/credential/codex-sync.ts`, `packages/core/src/integration.ts` resolve path, `packages/ai/src/providers/*-auth.ts`, `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/{openai,opencode}.ts`), CLI credential files (timestamps/lengths only), route_attempt serving evidence (last 24h), quota gatherer records.

## How renewal works in this fork (the two paths)

- **In-provider refresh:** `Integration.connection.resolve` refreshes any stored OAuth credential within 5 min of expiry, when its method implements `refresh` — **unless** the credential is stamped `externalRefresh`, in which case an external owner is the sole refresher (by design, to avoid rotating a shared refresh-token lineage twice).
- **External-owner sync:** CodexSync runs every 1 min, copies `~/.codex/auth.json` into the stored credential **whose account ID matches the file's account** (selectTarget), and stamps it `externalRefresh`. One account's tokens are never written into another account's credential.

## Per-provider table

Deliberately NOT CodexSync's target — different account than the CLI file | **SELF-RENEWS (proven)** | Row refresh-write 2026-11-04T22:05:48Z (expiry +10d exactly) during continuous service; 2,175 successful attempts in the last 24h on that lineage; no externalRefresh stamp | 2026-11-14T22:05:48Z (auto-refreshes at resolve) |
| opencode-go.popesdrew | OAuth (Console) | credential row `cred_1a1bd3e0…` (base `opencode` row is the same lineage, same expiry) | In-provider refresh at resolve (opencode plugin implements refresh, writes back the rotated pair) | **SELF-RENEWS-UNPROVEN** | Mechanism in deployed source; row untouched since creation 2026-11-04 — no refresh event has occurred yet. Acceptance check: row `time_updated` advances on first resolve at/after ~2026-12-03T17:37Z with no human step | 2026-12-03T17:42:29Z |
| opencode-go.drewrypope | API key | credential row | — | **NO-RENEWAL-NEEDED** | 3,296 successes / 24h | — |

Acceptance check: file mtime/expiresAt advance past the access expiry with no human or CLI step. | google (OAuth row `cred_12e4e76…`) | OAuth | credential row | Door disabled in config; access token expired 2026-10-12, refresh token still held | **DORMANT** — not serving; no live defect. If the door is ever re-enabled, first resolve must be watched: the row has been expired for a month | Row untouched since 2026-10-12 | access expired 2026-10-12T05:10:53Z |
| github-copilot | OAuth | credential row + auth.json | Door disabled in config | **DORMANT** — not serving | Last success 2026-10-24 (legacy id) | none recorded |
| opencode (base row) | OAuth | credential row | Disabled integration; same token lineage and expiry as opencode-go.popesdrew | **DORMANT duplicate** of the popesdrew door row | Identical expiry to the second (2026-12-03T17:42:29Z) | 2026-12-03T17:42:29Z |

## Findings

1. **Zero CANNOT-RENEW defects among live doors.** After tonight's three fixes, every serving door either self-renews, holds a static key, or has a configured renewal that has not yet had its first natural test.
2. **Three SELF-RENEWS-UNPROVEN doors, each with a dated acceptance check:** opencode-go.popesdrew (first refresh due at the 2026-12-03 expiry approach), _claude (first rotation due at the 2026-11-10T10:28:53Z access expiry — today), _muse (re-mint unobserved; account-token expiry uninstrumented, watched by the meta-renewal validator). If any acceptance check fails, it becomes a CANNOT-RENEW defect on sight.
3. **Hygiene observations (not renewal defects):** (a) the legacy `claude-code` credential row holds stub-length tokens from 2026-10-05 and the legacy provider id drew 9 auth-failing attempts in 24h (last 2026-11-10T00:14Z, pre-restore) — the live _claude door never reads this row; recommend deleting the stub row and retiring the legacy id. (b) The dormant `google` OAuth row (above). (c) The base `opencode` row duplicates the popesdrew lineage.
4. **Quota-side browser sessions are a separate surface**, already owned by #6120 (OpenDesign keeper landed; Meta portal re-capture requirement sits on #6079; ClinePass dashboard adapter dormant by design). This audit covers serving credentials; #6120 covers the monitoring reads. Cross-linked, not duplicated.

items.title: feat(id): BIP39-style seed-phrase export/restore for the identity key (#2381)
items.body: ## What The seed-phrase slice of #2381 (umbrella: encrypted identity backup), dispatched after slice 1 (#2279, PR #5322) landed the passphrase envelope: - **`id key export-seed [--client]`** prints the identity key as a 24-word seed phrase, once, to the terminal — never to a file, never taken or shown on a command line — with handling warnings (the phrase IS the key). - **`id key import-seed [--client] [--replace]`** restores the identity from the phrase entered at a hidden prompt, writing the key file through the same no-clobber / atomic-replace helpers as envelope import. - **New `seed_phrase` module**: a direct BIP39 encoding of the key's 32 bytes — entropy + SHA-256 checksum bits, 11-bit word packing, the official 2048-word English list embedded verbatim (`seed_wordlist.txt`, from the BIP39 spec repo). Decoding is strict: unknown words (named by position), non-BIP39 word counts, and checksum mismatches all refuse, and case/whitespace are normalized the way a person pastes. All BIP39 entropy lengths (16–32 bytes) encode/decode; key restore requires exactly 32 bytes (24 words). Design note: the phrase encodes the key bytes directly rather than feeding a KDF — restoring must recover the exact identity secret, and the checksum is an integrity check, not a password. No second envelope format is introduced; this sits beside `key_envelope` and shares its conventions (zeroized key material, hidden prompts, no secrets on argv). The OPRF server-backup slice and the restore-forces-rotation flag (gated on #2380) remain on #2381 as later slices, per its ordering. ## Tests `cargo test -p id --lib` (filtered): - `seed_phrase`: 7 tests — official BIP39 vectors (0x00…→ abandon×23+art, 0xff…→ zoo×23+vote, 0x7f… 16-byte prefix), wordlist invariants (2048 words, unique 4-letter prefixes), round-trip, case/whitespace normalization, checksum-mismatch / unknown-word / bad-count refusals, 24-word requirement for keys. - `commands::key` existing import/clobber tests pass; `cli::tests::test_cli_parse_key_export_and_import` extended with `export-seed` / `import-seed` parse assertions and passes. Refs #2381 (acceptance item 1). --- Open in [code]smith · Need help on this PR? Tag @codesmith-bot with what you need.

items.title: feat(id): flag a key restored from backup until a keyset rotation retires it (#2381)
items.body: Before: a key brought back with `id key import` or `id key import-seed` worked silently, though a restore may follow theft and #2381 asks that restore force or prompt a rotation. After: both imports print a warning and leave a restore marker naming the restored key. The key stays flagged until a keyset rotation retires it, meaning the identity's keyset no longer lists it as an active admin key. `id keyset` reports the flag after every command and clears it once the rotation lands. `id serve` logs a warning at start while it's pending. The flag warns and never blocks the key, because a restore is also how an owner gets back in. How: new `id_directory::restored_key` (marker files `.id-key-restored` and `.id-key-client-restored`, `settle`, read-only `pending`), plus `KeysetFile::open_existing` so serve can read the keyset without migrating it. Tests cover no marker, flagged with no keyset, still flagged after migration, cleared after rotation, and a keyset for another identity not clearing it. `cargo test -p id-directory --lib -- restored_key keyset_file`: 9 passed. `cargo test -p id-cli --lib -- commands::key commands::keyset`: 3 passed. This is the restore-forces-rotation slice of #2381. The OPRF server-backup slice is still open there, so this doesn't close it. --- _Generated by [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/code/session_01YLT5JyFdZgVpkFFqSHMPHV)_ --- Open in [code]smith · Need help on this PR? items.body:
Filed by the 2026-11-23 repo sweep (all repos/worktrees in sandbox + laptop homes). The sweep landed what it safely could and deleted 213 verified-done worktrees. The items below were deliberately left in place because they hold state that exists nowhere else or needs an owner's judgment. Nothing here was discarded.

## 1. Queue-task worktrees with local-only tip commits (largest class)
~200 worktrees under `~/git/fleet/` and sibling areas (code parent: 133 in the fleet bucket alone; opencode parent: 44; openchamber parent: 24) are clean but their HEAD commit is on NO remote ref — typically 1–2 commits from Nov 7–11 task runs. Sampling shows the class is MIXED: `fleet/11051-6831`'s tip is patch-equivalent to landed work (`git cherry` `-`), but `fleet/11065-6847`'s two commits (fix + property tests for #6847) are NOT in main in that form (`git cherry` `+`). Do not bulk-delete; each needs a cherry check or an owner decision.

items.body:
## PM push unification — one registry, one sender, the Android app as a first-class endpoint

**Drew's order (2026-11-23):** "start a lane now to unify push between the like 2 pm stack locations and the pm stack android app."

**Full design of record:** dated doc record `doc/2026-11-24T04-45-43Z_design_pm-push-unification/` (doc-only PR linked below when landed). This body is the faithful summary; the doc record governs.

### Premise check — the landscape is worse than "two locations" (verified 2026-11-23, code + live stores)

There are **four Web Push senders, three subscription stores (+ one mirror), three VAPID keypairs, and two incompatible class/preference models**:

| Location | Store (live count) | Classes | Sender / keys | Surfaces |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Aggregator** (laptop, `pm-stack/aggregator`) | Turso `alerts.push_subscriptions` — **0** (2026-11-23, #14048); sends ledger `alerts.notification_sends` — 271 rows, none after 2026-11-17, 269/269 undated per the roll-up (#14061) | 8 toggleable: `incident`, `needs-drew`, `quota-wall`, `quota-near-wall`, `section-risk`, `stack-health`, `blocked-age`, `prompt` (+ `digest` as a delivery shape) | `web-push` library; VAPID pair **A** (public key in code, private in Bitwarden by name) | `/alerts`, `/alerts/preferences`, `/notifications` at the tailnet URL |
| **Console origin** (laptop, `pm-stack/console` `src/server.ts`) | File store `~/.local/state/pm-console/push.json` — **0** (live count tonight) | 4: `replies`, `needs`, `questions`, `trouble` — toggled by a **store-global** off-list, not per subscription | Hand-rolled RFC 8291/8292 (`src/push.ts`); VAPID pair **B** in the store file | The console site at its origin; `GET /push` delivery status |
| **Console edge** (Cloudflare, `pm-stack/console/edge`) | KV store (`kvStore(kv, "push")`) — **count not readable from the laptop**; no census route exists | Same 4 (same code) | Same hand-rolled sender, VAPID pair **C** held in the KV store document | `pm.security.cab` — the live site the Android app wraps |
| **Notify-relay** (Cloudflare DO, `pm-stack/notify-relay`, #8569) | Mirror of the aggregator's full set (snapshot POST on change, seq-ordered) | Sends only `stack.silent` + recovered, riding `incident` | Own `push.ts`, reusing pair **A** (private key as a Worker secret) | `GET /status` only |

**The Android app** (`pm-stack/console/android`, package `today.developing.pmconsole`) is a Trusted Web Activity over the console site: it has **no push channel of its own** — the *console's* Web Push arrives as the app's notifications. Its widget polls a summary every ~30 min on a separate read-only device token (`console/src/devices.ts`), an identity registry unrelated to push subscriptions.

**Consequences, plainly:**
- The app Drew actually uses can only ever receive the console's 4 classes. The answerable `needs-drew` pushes (the ones #14043's write-back serves), the quota family, `section-risk`, `stack-health`, `blocked-age`, `prompt` can only reach an aggregator browser subscription — of which there are currently **zero**.
- #14048 ("delivery dark") and #14061 ("pushes do reach Drew's phone") are **both true — of different stacks**.
- Nobody can answer "how many live push endpoints exist?" — the edge KV store has no census route, and the other two stores are both empty.
- Class models diverge: the aggregator's preferences are per-subscription (class map + quiet hours); the console's are store-global. Twelve distinct class ids exist across the stacks with near-miss overlaps (`needs` vs `needs-drew`, `trouble` vs `incident`/`stack-health`).
- #14061's blindness is structural: `AlertsStore.logSend`'s insert names **no timestamp column** — the send time rides on a column default in a SQL-translated store, and the roll-up's parser rejects what the live rows carry (269/269 excluded).

### The design (summary — doc record governs)

1. **One registry.** `push_endpoints` + per-endpoint preference rows in the fleet-platform Turso store — hosted, already the aggregator's store, and reachable from the console edge over HTTPS (the same store family the edge already uses for decision sets). An endpoint row names its **transport** (`webpush`), its **client** (`browser` | `android-app`), an optional link to the console device registry, label, user agent, created/last-seen, gone count. The Android app's TWA-held subscription registers as an endpoint in its own right — named, countable, preference-bearing as the app — and the transport column is where a future native (FCM) transport lands without redesign.
2. **One sender.** A single send service owning VAPID pair **A**; every producer submits candidates to it. The aggregator engine and the console Notifier both become producers into the one candidate path (dedupe/cooldown/fingerprint/quiet-hours machinery is the aggregator's, reused). The notify-relay keeps pair A and its mirror as the designed exception — a sender of last resort whose whole purpose is the primary being down. Console origin + edge `Push` instances retire as senders; pairs B and C retire with them.
3. **One class taxonomy.** The union of the 12 ids, each with exactly one producer of record. `needs` (console census-diff: new needs-me items) and `needs-drew` (answerable attention-tier questions) stay **distinct ids with distinct labels** in v1 — merging them is a product decision flagged below, not an engineering default. `stack.silent` remains a payload variant of `incident` at the relay. `digest` remains a delivery shape, never a class.
4. **One preference model.** Per-endpoint class map + quiet hours (the aggregator's model — the richer one). The console's store-global off-list migrates onto its endpoints' maps. One preferences surface, served from the console (pm.security.cab — where Drew and the app live), backed by the registry; the aggregator's `/alerts/preferences` keeps working during migration, then redirects there.
5. **Event-driven at detection.** Producers emit at their detection points (broker/watchdog raises, quota snapshot transitions, console state-doc diffs, relay alarm) into the candidate intake — per Drew's standing requirement, the stack pushes itself; no new polling loops are introduced.
6. **Answerable pushes unchanged.** The `needs-drew` payload contract (ledger id + options + per-question answer landing) is preserved exactly, and must work identically when the endpoint is the app (the TWA already intercepts pm.security.cab links). Answer *application* remains #14043's territory; edge answer intake (#13469) composes unchanged.
7. **Delivery observability by construction.** One sends ledger in the registry store: one row per attempt, `sent_at` stamped **by the writer** (ISO-8601 UTC, schema-required — never a column default again), endpoint id, class, object ref, outcome incl. push-service status, `acted_on_at` via the existing Ack transition. Two designed-in alarms: **undated-row alarm** (any row the roll-up cannot date is a data defect that pages — this subsumes #14061's alarm ask for the unified ledger; #14061 remains the vehicle for the legacy ledger's repair/backfill) and the **zero-endpoint sentinel** (#14048's detection ask): zero live endpoints while undelivered incidents exist — or no successful send in N days with incidents open — raises a stack-health incident on a **non-push** surface, because a push about no-push is a dead letter by definition. A census read (endpoints by transport/client + last successful send) is exposed on both stacks' status surfaces: one answer to "how many live endpoints?"

### Migration

- Aggregator subscriptions: none live — nothing to move; its schema shape seeds the registry.
- Console edge subscriptions **cannot be re-keyed**: a Web Push subscription is bound to the application-server key used at subscribe time, so pair-C subscriptions cannot be carried to pair A as rows. Migration is a **re-subscription**: the console site/app detects the sender-key change via its existing endpoint-mark mechanism (built for exactly this — "so the app can tell that this sender has lost it") and re-subscribes under pair A into the registry. The KV store freezes read-only for one release, then drops. Console origin store: empty — retired outright.
- Relay mirror source switches from the aggregator store to the registry (same snapshot protocol, same secret by name).
- Legacy sends ledger stays as-is under #14061; the unified ledger starts at cutover and the `/notifications` roll-up reads it from then on.

### Boundaries

Not this design's: #14043 (answer write-back — untouched), #13469 (edge answer intake — composes), #8570 (service consolidation — the sender's natural eventual home, not a prerequisite), native FCM/APNs transport (v2 option the registry's transport column reserves), #14061's legacy-ledger backfill (linked, not duplicated).

### Build-slice map (ordered; **not packetised** — reason below)

- **S1 — Registry + aggregator adoption.** Unified endpoint/preference tables in fleet-platform Turso; `AlertsStore` reads/writes them; `/alerts/preferences` unchanged externally. Proof: aggregator notification test suite + a live subscribe → test-send on the laptop.
- **S2 — Unified sends ledger + observability.** Writer-stamped `sent_at`; roll-up on the unified ledger; undated-row alarm; zero-endpoint sentinel wired into stack-health (lands #14048's detection ask); census read. Needs S1.
- **S3 — Sender consolidation.** Console Notifier becomes a producer to the one sender (pair A); console origin `Push` retires. Proof: the 4 console classes delivered by the unified sender to a browser endpoint. Needs S1.
- **S4 — Edge cutover + app endpoint.** Edge `Push` retires as sender; subscribe path writes the registry with client + device link; endpoint-mark-driven re-subscription under pair A; the one preferences surface on pm.security.cab; `/alerts/preferences` redirect. Needs S3.
- **S5 — Relay re-point + close-out.** Mirror source = registry; legacy stores frozen/dropped; closure evidence for #14048/#14061 (census ≥ 1 live endpoint per class path; a week of dated sends). Needs S4.

**Why no packet yet:** two seams must be settled on this record before any slice is specified exactly — (i) the `needs`/`needs-drew` taxonomy call is Drew-facing (it changes what his toggles say) and is posed here for his word; (ii) S4's re-subscription slice can only be specified against the endpoint-mark flow's behaviour in the *shipped* app build, which the S3/S4 builder must verify live first. S1/S2 are close to specifiable and packetise on this design's acceptance — the #14043 pattern (design of record first, build slices from it).

### Open questions for Drew

1. Class taxonomy: keep `needs` and `needs-drew` as separate toggles (recommended — different promises: "new items need your hands" vs "a question only you can answer"), or merge into one "Needs you" class?
2. Preferences surface home: console (pm.security.cab) as the one surface, aggregator page redirecting — as designed — or the reverse?

— Lane PUSH-UNIFY, 2026-11-24. Progress + records on this issue at each boundary.

5. **NVIDIA — finish the setup.**
   - (a) Key hunt: config comments claim a stored, probe-verified key, but no `nvidia` name appears in `fleet secrets list` (same gap for `groq` and `openrouter`). Find the real locations (BWS under other names, laptop credential stores). If a key genuinely does not exist, create/rotate at the provider and store in BWS under the canonical name. Values never printed anywhere.
   - (b) **Answer, recorded here: is the NVIDIA free quota per-model or shared across the account?** (From NVIDIA's own docs/API.)
   - (c) Seat the free catalog (83 models) round-robin — the `google-free` round-robin route is the pattern — free-first in every pool the models fit. Probe per model before seating (config warns `kimi-k2.6` and `nemotron-3-super-120b` answered 404 for our account). Non-chat models (VL, embeddings, rerank) are NOT force-seated as chat; list them here for the DECISION-API lane's designation pass (#13675).
6. **OpenAI data sharing — APPROVED by Drew in this order** ("if openai gives away free tokens use them I'll share any and all data"). Verify eligibility first (ZDR/Enterprise orgs are excluded per the program terms — if this org is ineligible, record exactly that and stop this slice). Opt the `openai-payg` org in; once active, seat the program's models per its terms, free-first.
7. **EXAONE rotation plan** — free key expires **2026-12-16**. Record the expiry + rotation procedure (new key at provider → vault swap under the same name → credential-store row → verify) and a one-shot scheduled check ahead of the deadline (~2026-12-10) that performs or prompts the rotation.
8. **Verification** — a real live probe completion through the route for each of NVIDIA, Groq, OpenRouter, recorded with evidence. Every free model that fits a purpose seated. Groq note: chat free TPM (7–8K) can't carry a session's ~26K first request — tiny-prompt seats only; Groq's purpose shelf (Whisper STT, TTS, prompt-guard) belongs to #13675's designation work, not force-seated as chat.
9. **Free-first ordering pass** — across ALL pools, wherever a free leg can serve the pool's purpose, it leads. Standing route rule per Drew's order.

The DECISION-API lane (#13675) is editing the same config (designations + endpoints) concurrently. Config edits are serialized through the tracking issues: whoever reaches the config edit second rebases on the landed result. No parallel config edits.
