items.title: pm-stack(aggregator): /board, /api/board.json, /api/overview.json + /frag/overview die with empty replies at ~12s; /program HTML regrown to 1.16MB

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

items.body:
Filed by the pool-quota-steward follow-through (Drew, 2026-11-03: "/program and board are both fucked up and something needs to watch them; it might as well be steward"). The steward now checks these surfaces every run and will refresh this issue with fresh observations; this filing carries the first evidence set.

## Symptoms (laptop, aggregator on 127.0.0.1:4870, direct Bun server — no proxy in front)

- `GET /board` and `GET /api/board.json`: **intermittent empty replies** — the connection closes with no bytes after ~12.0s. Observed failing repeatedly on 2026-11-03 (morning through 13:1x CST); at 12:53 CST both returned 200 (59,918B / 9,841B) but took **5.1s**; at ~13:12 CST both died again at **12.001s / 12.002s** (curl exit 52, 0 bytes).
- `GET /api/overview.json` and `GET /frag/overview`: same failure family — empty reply at **12.000s** (observed 13:09–13:12 CST). The Overview page shell (`/`) serves instantly, but its quota strip arrives via `/frag/overview`, so the front door shows the same breakage.
- `GET /program`: serves 200 fast (0.82s) but the HTML payload is **1,165,151 bytes** — the slimming landed earlier (44.3MB → 716KB) has regressed by ~63%. `/api/program.json` is 65,931B and fast.

## Failure point (as far as identified)

- The dying routes share one assembly: `/api/overview.json` is `deriveOverview(await overviewContext())` (src/server.ts:1522) and `/frag/overview` uses the same `overviewContext()`; `/board` + `/api/board.json` render the board facet of the same context family. Quota-only routes (`/api/quota.json`, `/quota`) answer in ~0.03s, so the quota path is NOT the slow part.
- The cutoff is suspiciously exact (~12.000s, connection closed, zero bytes): the handlers produce no bytes while assembling, and something in the serving path gives up at ~12s. `Bun.serve` is configured with no explicit idleTimeout (src/server.ts:1928). Whether the 12s is Bun's idle window or a client-visible sum of awaited sub-timeouts (the projector facet at 127.0.0.1:7801 has an 8s timeout; projects.ts uses 20s; supabase.ts 60s), the assembly intermittently exceeds it — at 5.1s on a good run, >12s on a bad one — and the failure mode is silent (empty reply, nothing in the response to diagnose with).
- Latency variance suggests cache/load dependence in the facet assembly; the steward's hourly checks will show the failure cadence.

## What is NOT being asked here

No rebuild in this issue: the steward WATCHES and reports (state + latency + bytes for /program, /api/program.json, /board, /api/board.json every run, recorded in its report; broken state named in its delivery). This issue is the evidence home. Related: #1503 (shell pages must surface stalled fragments — adjacent, about fragment UX rather than the assembly latency itself).

## Acceptance shape (for whoever picks it up)

/board, /api/board.json, /api/overview.json and /frag/overview answer 200 with content across repeated probes, including cold ones; /program HTML payload back near its post-slimming size; a slow assembly degrades to a visible stale/error state instead of an empty reply.

items.title: cold-store-reaper v1: Google Drive cold-store CLI (pack / resumable upload+verify / range fetch)
items.body: ## What New `pkgs/cold-store-reaper/`: a stdlib-only Python 3.12 CLI that archives files into Google Drive as a cold, immutable store and restores individual objects back out. Commands: `init`, `auth-url`, `auth-exchange`, `ensure-folders`, `pack`, `upload`, `fetch`, `status`. ## Design points - **Bundle format:** each input file becomes its own zstd frame (via the `zstd` CLI); frames are concatenated into `b_.csb`. Bundles are immutable — a changed set is a new bundle. - **Manifest:** local SQLite using the canonical cold-store schema verbatim (`schema.sql` in the package): objects / bundles / members (byte offset+length per frame) / transfer_ledger / meta (3 TiB budget, 700 GB/day upload hard stop). - **Upload** is resumable + chunked; after completion it compares Drive's `md5Checksum`+size against local values and only then marks the bundle `verified`, flips its objects to `cold`, and writes a ledger row. - **Fetch** Range-downloads exactly one object's frame, decompresses it, and verifies the object sha256 before writing output. - **Identity:** the OAuth app holds ONLY the `drive.file` scope, so it can see nothing but files it creates. On first run it creates its own root folder `Cold Store Reaper` (subfolders `bundles/`, `manifests/`, `db-backups/`) and remembers IDs in `state.json`. Trees created by other apps are invisible to it and are never referenced by ID. - **Credentials:** `client_id`/`client_secret`/`refresh_token` live in a mode-600 `credentials.json` under `$COLD_STORE_HOME` (default `~/.config/cold-store/`), materialized by the operator from Bitwarden; secret values are never printed or committed. No real Google API calls are made by this PR or its tests (no grant exists yet). ## Tests ``` $ python3 -m unittest discover -s pkgs/cold-store-reaper/tests -v Ran 7 tests in ~20s — OK ``` All tests run offline against a fake Drive HTTP server (token endpoint, folder create/list, resumable upload sessions incl. 308 resume, files.get md5/size, Range downloads): - `TestAuth`: consent URL shape (scope/access_type/prompt/redirect); exchange stores the refresh token at mode 600 without echoing it. - `TestPack`: manifest rows, member offsets, frame extraction by offset/length, decompress+sha256 round-trip. - `TestUploadFetch`: ensure-folders idempotence; multi-chunk upload -> verified (Drive md5 matches) -> objects cold -> fetch round-trip byte-identical; ledger rows for both directions; unknown-object fetch errors. - `TestStatus`: counts/cold-bytes arithmetic, rolling-24h ledger window (a 3-day-old row is excluded), hard-stop + budget flags. Also smoke-tested the real CLI offline: `init` -> `pack` -> `status` against a temp `$COLD_STORE_HOME`. ## Not in v1 R2-eviction reaper loop, DB-backup path, rehydrator Worker path, compaction — later steps of the design's build order. --- Need help on this PR? Tag @codesmith-bot with what you need.

items.title: atlas search worker: Cloudflare Worker + per-query Durable Object embedding/result cache over the shard fan-out (successor surface for #5755)
items.body:
## What Drew ordered (2026-11-06 22:48 CST, verbatim substance)

Build the cross-database search surface as a **Cloudflare Worker** that pulls **all databases** for search; for each search query it **stores a Durable Object**, **automatically inserts the query as an embedding**, and **caches the result — for now, indefinitely** (no TTL/expiry).

This is the successor surface for the Atlas shard consumer wiring in #5755 (slice 1 merged in #6661; rehomed as `fleet serve search` in #6674). It supersedes the 2026-11-05 "Ask-the-ledger" direction (Cloudflare AI Search / AutoRAG over R2 snapshots + a query/miss ledger DB): Drew replaced the managed-AI-Search design with this explicit Worker + Durable Object + embedding cache design. The AI Search proposal is **not** being built; this issue is the record of what replaced it.

## Architecture (v1)

**Components**

1. **Cloudflare Worker** (`pkgs/atlas-search/worker/`) — the only public edge. Inbound gate: a shared bearer secret checked in the Worker (constant-time compare); not public-open. (Cloudflare Access in front of the Worker hostname is a follow-up hardening note below.)
2. **Durable Object class `QueryCache`** — one DO per distinct query. DO name = `sha256(normalized_query || config_fingerprint)` where the fingerprint pins `{ceiling: "personal", model_rev, vec_table, trunc: 0, k}` so a cache entry can never be served across different effective ceilings or embedding spaces (the same rule the search service applies to job dedupe).
3. **The fleet search service** (`fleet serve search` / `atlas-search serve`, laptop loopback :18760) remains the fan-out engine: it discovers the shard set from the Turso Platform API (only `atlas-core-*` databases), reads each candidate's `atlas_manifest` self-description (tier, topic, part, expected chunks), enforces per-client tier ceilings, embeds the query with the one shared resident embedder, runs the parallel cosine scan + merge/rerank. **The Worker keeps no shard list of its own** — new databases join the fan-out by existing in the Turso org with the `atlas-core-` prefix and a manifest; the Worker inherits the set through the service.
4. **Reachability**: the service is exposed to the Worker through the existing `amd-6-pm-stack` Cloudflare Tunnel as `atlas-search.security.cab` → `localhost:18760`, fronted by a Cloudflare Access application whose only policy is a **service token** the Worker presents (`CF-Access-Client-Id`/`CF-Access-Client-Secret`). The tunnel hostname without the service token is rejected by Access before it reaches the laptop.

**Miss path** (first time a query is seen)

1. Worker normalizes the query, computes the DO key, asks the DO for its entry → miss.
2. Worker calls the service's new **`POST /v1/embed`** (added by this work to both `server.rs` copies, parity-guarded): the service's shared embedder returns the production query vector. The Worker stores `{query, normalized_query, embedding, model, model_rev, dims, created_at}` in the DO **first** — the DO is born holding the query's embedding, per Drew's spec, even if the search below then fails.
3. Worker calls `POST /v1/search` (sync one-shot) with the dedicated **`cf-worker` service client** (see boundary below) → merged, reranked results.
4. Worker stores `{result, searched_at, fanout_ms, embed_ms}` in the DO and returns the result with `cache: "miss"` and the timings.

**Hit path**

- The DO returns the stored result verbatim; the fleet service is never contacted. Response carries `cache: "hit"`, the original `searched_at`, and a `hit_count` the DO increments. This is the proof surface: a hit must be byte-identical to the miss response's result and must not move any counter on the service side.

**Retention**

- **Indefinite.** No TTL, no eviction in v1 — Drew's "for now". DO storage is the ledger of every query ever asked through this surface. A future eviction policy (size/LRU) is a deliberate follow-up (filed separately), not a v1 behavior.

## Embedding source — decision and why

**The fleet embedder** (the service's resident ONNX session): model `Snowflake/snowflake-arctic-embed-m-v2.0` pinned at rev `95c2741480856aa9666782eb4afe11959938017f`, query prompt `"query: "`, production vector table `vec_snowflake_m_v2_768_f32` — **768 dimensions**, full width (trunc = 0).

**Workers AI is rejected**: its 384-dim `@cf/baai/bge-small-en-v1.5` lives in a different embedding space (and a different width). Cosine similarity across embedding spaces is meaningless; a Worker-side embedding that cannot be compared against the corpus vectors would silently corrupt every ranking. Any edge embedding must reproduce the corpus's exact space, and the only artifact that does that today is the pinned Snowflake session in the fleet service.

Correction to older notes: several records describe the corpus as "384-dim Snowflake". Production is **768-dim** (`vec_snowflake_m_v2_768_f32` in the live service config; 384 was a Matryoshka truncation option from the Python era, never the production width).

## Secret-tier boundary

- The Worker authenticates to the search service as a dedicated client, **`cf-worker`, with `ceiling_cap: "personal"`** — the service mechanically caps it to the Public + Internal tiers. The Secret tier is unreachable through this client no matter what the Worker asks for.
- The Worker holds **no Turso credentials** and never receives secret-tier shard data, so nothing secret can enter a Durable Object — neither chunk content nor embeddings of secret chunks.
- The `drew-cli` client (`secret-bearing` cap) stays laptop-local and is not used by anything in this build. Secret-tier search remains a laptop-side-only operation, exactly as today.

## What v1 deliberately leaves out

- **Filters / FTS interplay** — the fan-out runs the service's default hybrid search; classification/date filters and the FTS answer remain #6665.
- **Hydration (`--expand`)** — results are the service's standard envelope; expansion remains #6664.
- **Serve-mode snapshot-id integration** — remains #6666.
- **Eviction policy** for the indefinite cache — follow-up issue (Drew: "for now").
- **Access in front of the Worker hostname itself** — v1 gate is the in-Worker bearer check; recorded as a hardening follow-up.
- The live proof in this issue advances #6662 only for the `personal` ceiling path through the Worker; #6662 stays open for its remaining parity scope.

## Open questions (recorded, proceeded on defaults)

- Worker hostname: default `atlas-search` on the account's `workers.dev` subdomain; a custom domain can be bound later without changing the design.
- Whether the DO should also store the FTS match expression / branch pools for debugging: default no — result + embedding + provenance only.

## Proof required (acceptance)

- Deployed Worker + DO; a real query run twice: first response `cache: "miss"` with fan-out executed (service-side evidence), DO created holding a 768-dim embedding; second response `cache: "hit"`, byte-identical result, served from the DO with no service contact; timings for both; DO state read back through the Worker's gated inspect endpoint.

items.body:
Drew's directive, 2026-11-04: documentation and designs that are **not strictly about the sandbox environment** move their canonical home from dezren39/hatch-personal + dezren39/hatch into this repo; darwin-nix keeps only flake documentation. We're aggregating docs and productionizing the binaries — designs that led to built things live together here. **Plan + issues only in this step; no files have moved yet.**

Full plan + machine-readable inventory (sandbox workspace): `~/workspace/scratch/docs-migration-plan-2026-11-04/plan.md` + `inventory.json`.

## Classification standard

Every tracked item is exactly one of:

- **MOVE** — canonical home becomes code.
- **STAY** — sandbox-environment / system-baked (init script, quota script, prompts, AGENTS.md, avatars, TOOLS.md/TOOLS.d; in darwin-nix: flake mechanics + functional config/code).
- **STAY-UNTIL-REPLACED** — register below; each names the missing fleet feature that is its exit condition.

Test: *would this make sense to someone running the fleet/code without this sandbox?* darwin-nix specialisation: docs **about** a topic move; flake code/config that **uses** the topic stays.

**Copy, never delete.** Source repos keep historical copies permanently; living docs get a one-line `Canonical:` pointer header in the source after the copy lands.

## Counts (tracked files)

| Repo | Total | MOVE | STAY-UNTIL-REPLACED | STAY |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| hatch-personal (482) / hatch public mirror (475 = same set − 7 submodule entries) | 482 | 110 | 18 | 354 |
| darwin-nix | 474 | 32 | 0 | 442 |

## Batches

- #5976 — backup scripts & backup documentation (27 files: runtime-db-export, bws-backup-secrets, backup process docs)
- #5978 — Fleet designs, task-system schema & fleet machinery (42 files: 29 Supabase migrations, fleet-fetch, archer-slack design, mcpx-opencode plan; fleet-brokers already migrated via #5430)
- #5980 — architecture & how-it-works docs, DB/platform tooling (25 files: supabase-exec, turso-exec, Cloudflare tooling, toolchain docs, platform research)
- #5981 — Atlas documentation sweep (zero Atlas docs exist in the repos — they live in untracked workspace/research locations; this batch enumerates + sweeps them into `doc/`)
- #5982 — darwin-nix non-flake docs (32 files: mcpx designs + services docs, agent-workflow docs)

## Stay-until-replaced register

- **R1** — laptop-ssh fallback family (8 files) → #5972 (fleet built-in fallback connection mode)
- **R2** — oc-attach family (3 files) → #1357 (existing; attach-first client helper)
- **R3** — proxy-supervisor family (7 files, currently dormant) → #5974 (fleet serve built-in supervised local proxy endpoints)

## darwin-nix five-topic findings

- **mcpx**: 3 design plans + `docs/mcp.md` + `docs/services.md` move (#5982). `mcpx.config.nix` classified STAY (functional config) — **flagged for Drew**: if "anything about mcpx" includes the config, its exit is config generated from code, a bigger change.
- **ID**: no ID documentation in darwin-nix.
- **Atlas**: none — all hits are *Atlassian* false positives.
- **Cloudflare**: zero hits. **Turso**: zero hits.

## Borderline (classified in the plan, needs Drew's eye)

`docs/feed.md` (STAY as platform doc vs your "news agent" example — no doc about *our* news agent exists in the repos); mcpx sections inside darwin-nix `ROADMAP.md`/`ARCHITECTURE.md` (trim to pointers after #5982); darwin-nix `archive/` vendored skills (STAY); darwin-nix planning/commands/tool-definitions (MOVE, 22 files); hatch `library/toolchains/nix.md` + `muse-cli.md`; hatch queue artifacts (`lane-*.sh`, repo-task schema); hatch `library/skills/`; hatch `notes/research/muse/`.

## Longer-term direction (recorded, not this migration)

All docs + Zettelkasten notes + conversation logs + notes from various places eventually integrate into Atlas + the Zettelkasten graph / ID system with classifications; a technical-reference / beginner's-guide website may be backed by objects tagged for that site (repo- or DB-backed, undecided). Code is the best home now and makes that later move easier.

items.title: Atlas repo docs and design archive disagreements: README index, who serves, CI triggers, census freshness, endpoint table (book survey, #13251)
items.body:
Found by the Atlas book survey (#13251, survey D). Disagreements in the repo's own Atlas documentation and design archive. The book (pkgs/atlas-search/book/) now carries the reconciled account; these are the stale sources.

1. **doc/README.md indexes 6 Atlas records; doc/ contains 38 Atlas entries.** Most of the design archive — including the design of record, scaler revision, staging gate, classification, metadata, D1-cache and embedded-replica records — has no README entry, while one README entry (the lawyer packet) has no "atlas" in its directory name. A reader navigating by the README misses ~85% of the archive. (The book's roadmap chapter now maps all 38.)
2. **Design-of-record layout vs the package as built.** Design §4 proposes pkgs/atlas-search/ with a package-local doc/ and exactly four crates + fixtures/. The built package has docs/ (plural, three files), no package-local doc/, and substantial extra top-level surface the design tree does not show (atlas_search.py, worker/, eval/, schema/, tools/, tests/, test-vectors/, onnxruntime/).
3. **atlas_search.py points at a README that was not there; Python line count drift.** The Python header says "(see README.md in this directory)" — pkgs/atlas-search/ had no README.md (the book PR adds one, so the pointer now resolves). The design of record describes the Python as 1,177 lines (true of the hatch-personal copy); the in-repo copy is 1,629 lines. The two copies are not the same file version; "the Python reference" needs a which-copy qualifier.
4. **Who serves: design + unit name say atlas-search serve; the live ExecStart is fleet serve search** (#5604, atlasSearchServeViaFleet = true). The Worker README's deploy note ("a binary refresh of the laptop's atlas-search.service") is unit-accurate but binary-silent on this point.
5. **CI headers/names vs CI triggers (three workflows).** atlas-search-pr.yml is named for PRs but triggers on nightly schedule + dispatch only (deliberate policy; the name is the stale part). atlas-search-worker-tests.yml's header says it runs "on pushes to main that touch pkgs/atlas-search/worker/ and on dispatch"; its on: block is dispatch + nightly only. fleet-search-parity-guard.yml presents as a drift guard for a byte-parity contract but triggers on workflow_dispatch only — nothing runs it automatically, and the two server.rs copies already differ in size (151,924 vs 151,913 bytes), so "verbatim copy" in fleet-search/src/lib.rs reads as a maintained copy under parity discipline, not byte-identity.
6. **Program record names a package that does not exist.** The program investigation record describes "`pkgs/atlas-search/`, `pkgs/atlas-core` surfaces" — there is no pkgs/atlas-core; atlas-core is a crate inside pkgs/atlas-search/crates/.
7. **Two caches, opposite TTL stories, both called "the Atlas cache".** The service temp store: in-memory, 10-minute TTL / 60-minute hard cap, nothing survives restart by requirement (a security property). The Worker cache (#6805): Durable-Object-persisted, indefinite, no TTL/eviction in v1 (a cost property). Documents that do not name which store a TTL claim belongs to mislead; the book names them separately throughout.
8. **Embedding endpoint 18791 (memory design) vs in-process ONNX (everything else).** The memory-integration design routes ingestion embeddings through "the openclaw-embedding service, fixed loopback port 18791" or atlas-embed. No code, nix, or other doc in the Atlas estate references 18791; the built embedding is in-process ONNX resident in the serve process, and the service's outward embedding surface is POST /v1/embed on :18760 (#6788). The memory design's slice 2 does not describe the pipeline the service runs.
9. **Ingest: two generations described as current in different homes.** The turso-atlas README presents the collect→normalize→index→publish→access atlas-ingest.py pipeline as THE pipeline, present tense. The in-repo machinery describes per-unit staging DBs, a registry, classification-at-staging, an M6-gated promote and a five-stage batch gate; the scaler design's migration table says the aggregator path replaces direct-to-core ingest. The 2026-11-23 program record sides with the README on current practice (manual/script-driven; #5670 migration open) and with the in-repo design on target shape. The book states the generation labels once, early.
10. **Census freshness: the headline numbers are a 2026-10-31 snapshot repeated as present tense.** 18,325 / 122,124 / 107,639 appears in the design of record (2026-11-04) as current shape and is still the ground-truth line in the 2026-11-23 program record — which itself flags the store has grown (~7.3 GB monolith) without a verified recount. The design of record's "107,639 chunks in a Turso database" (monolith framing) and the program record's "monolith plus 29 topic shards" describe the same census at different physical-layout generations. The book dates the census 2026-10-31 everywhere.
11. **Design endpoint table vs the implemented route table.** Design §2's table has seven rows; the implemented server.rs dispatch adds POST /v1/embed, POST/GET /v1/feedback (+ unversioned aliases) and GET /v1/search/jobs. None contradicts the design, but an API chapter built from the design table alone would omit three live surfaces — including the one the Worker depends on.

Book chapters: pkgs/atlas-search/book/design/roadmap-and-issue-map.md (archive map), reference/service-api.md, concepts/ingest.md, operations/backup-and-census.md.

milestone.title: Fleet tool - one door, one binary
milestone.description: The fleet binaries as one tool: the `fleet` multicall binary epic (#5412) + queue-state unification (#8575 and its slices) + the laptop brokers (#5343/#5362 family), which the design folds in as `fleet serve` roles. Rolled up into one milestone by design.

items.body:
Epic: #5412 · Parent design: #5343 · Related: #5509 (dedicated RustDesk SSH forward)

## Context

Remote desktop to the laptop today works, but not through the fleet:

- **RustDesk (physical desktop)** goes over a dedicated raw SSH forward
  (`~/tools/rustdesk-gl/forward.sh`: sandbox `127.0.0.1:21118` → laptop
  `127.0.0.1:21118`, its own non-multiplexed `ssh -N -L`, isolated after
  #5509 root-caused freezes to contention on the shared laptop-ssh
  ControlMaster). It works and sessions run indefinitely, but it is a
  second, SSH-shaped transport beside the fleet brokers, with no pooling,
  no preconnect, and no place in the fleet services map.
- **Chrome Remote Desktop** (the `amd-crd` container on the laptop) gives
  a *virtual* desktop that shares the laptop's filesystem and is decoupled
  from the physical desktop login — which matters because laptop desktop
  login state has been a recurring blocker for the physical session. It
  is Google-brokered and is a separate world from the fleet.
- **Fleet proxy** is a TCP CONNECT proxy: `tunnel.rs` opens raw tunnels
  through the runtime egress proxy, `serve.rs` pools them per port
  (default 50) and pre-warms the laptop-agent pool at startup — but the
  broker protocol only carries HTTP request/response JSON for services
  (ports 4799/4800/4801 today), never a raw long-lived byte stream.
- **Sandbox constraint:** the sandbox reaches the tailnet only via the
  runtime proxy CONNECT — **TCP only, no UDP**. RustDesk's rendezvous /
  hole-punch machinery uses UDP heavily, so any fleet design must work
  in a TCP-only, relay/direct shape, not the hole-punch shape.

This issue answers, from RustDesk's actual docs/source: where the
secrets live, whether the broker can relay (and pre-warm) a desktop
transport without holding any of them, what concurrent clients mean on
a RustDesk host, and what per-connection virtual desktops would take.

Upstream sources used throughout:

- RustDesk self-host docs — <https://github.com/rustdesk/doc.rustdesk.com/blob/HEAD/content/self-host/_index.en.md>
- RustDesk advanced settings (`direct-server`, `direct-access-port`) — <https://RustDesk.Com/docs/en/self-host/client-configuration/advanced-settings/>
- RustDesk client/host source — <https://github.com/rustdesk/rustdesk/blob/master/src/client.rs>, <https://github.com/rustdesk/rustdesk/blob/master/src/server.rs>, <https://github.com/rustdesk/rustdesk/blob/master/src/server/connection.rs>, <https://github.com/rustdesk/rustdesk/blob/master/src/rendezvous_mediator.rs>
- RustDesk server source — <https://github.com/rustdesk/rustdesk-server/blob/master/src/rendezvous_server.rs> (`hbbs`), <https://github.com/rustdesk/rustdesk-server/blob/master/src/relay_server.rs> (`hbbr`)

Fleet sources are cited as `pkgs/fleet/…:line` in this repo.

## Findings (a) — Secrets, in three separate layers

RustDesk conflates easily; the layers are in fact cleanly separated:

**1. Rendezvous / ID registration (who is who).** Every host registers
with the ID server `hbbs` (TCP+UDP 21116): `RegisterPeer` announces the
peer ID + address; `RegisterPk` registers the peer's `uuid` and public
key, and `hbbs` stores `id → (uuid, pk, ip)` and hands the pk back out
*signed* (`signed_id_pk`) inside punch-hole / relay responses
(rustdesk-server `rendezvous_server.rs:396,412,488,596,709`).
What a rendezvous server holds: peer IDs, public keys, IPs — and its
own server signing key pair (the `key` clients pin in Settings →
Network). No session password is ever registered.

**2. Transport establishment (how bytes get there).** `hbbs` tries to
hole-punch A↔B (TCP 21116, UDP 21116, plus host-side TCP/UDP/KCP/WebRTC
punches). On failure both sides dial the relay `hbbr` (TCP 21117) with
`RequestRelay { uuid, licence_key }`; the first arrival waits in a
`PEERS` map (30 s pairing window) and the second with the same `uuid`
is spliced to it, `set_raw()` on both streams, opaque forwarding from
then on (rustdesk-server `relay_server.rs:461–492`).
What a relay needs: the pairing `uuid` (a per-connection nonce issued
via rendezvous), and *optionally* the server `licence_key` if `hbbr`
was started with `-k` — that key gates relay *use*, it is not the
session password. A relay needs **no peer password, no peer private
key, and does not even need the peer's public key** (the pk travels
client→client via the signed rendezvous response, not via `hbbr`).

**3. Session authentication (may this client drive the desktop).**
This happens **host-side, after transport, inside the connection** —
in the controlled host's `Connection` (rustdesk `src/server/connection.rs`):

- On open the host immediately sends `Hash { salt, challenge }`, the
  challenge freshly minted per connection
  (`Connection::start`, salt from the permanent-password config,
  `challenge: Config::get_auto_password(6)`; `on_open` sends the Hash,
  connection.rs:545–549, 1510–1531).
- The client answers in `LoginRequest.password` with the proof
  `SHA256( SHA256(password + salt) + challenge )`
  (client: `handle_hash` / `handle_login_from_ui`, client.rs:4647ff,
  4872ff; host: `verify_h1` / `validate_password_plain`,
  connection.rs:2523–2560). **The password itself is never sent, in
  cleartext or otherwise.**
- Which password is accepted is policy, not protocol:
  `verification-method` = temporary (the rotating one-time password
  shown on the host) / permanent / **both (default)**; crossed with
  `approve-mode` = password / click (person at the host approves) /
  **both (default `password-click`)** — `hbb_common`
  `password_security.rs:42–90`. Optional TOTP 2FA on the host gates
  authorization after the password proof.
- On the rendezvous/relay path the proof additionally travels **inside
  the encrypted session**: the client verifies the `hbbs`-signed peer
  pk (`decode_id_pk` against the pinned server key), generates a fresh
  symmetric session key, seals it to the host's ephemeral box pk
  (`create_symmetric_key_msg`), and the stream runs NaCl secretbox
  from then on (`secure_connection`, client.rs:1655ff; host side
  `identity_handshake`, server.rs:262ff). Password verification is
  therefore end-to-end: rendezvous sees identity, relay sees
  ciphertext, host alone checks the proof.

**Direct answer:** yes — a TCP transport to a RustDesk host can be
opened and its bytes relayed end-to-end **without anyone in the middle
holding, seeing, or being able to check the session password.** That
is exactly `hbbr`'s design, and a fleet CONNECT splice inherits it:
the broker needs a target host:port and nothing else. No token file,
no password in broker config, no password in broker logs — the broker
cannot parse the stream it splices.

**Two caveats that must be designed around, both from source:**

- **The direct-IP path is NOT the encrypted path.** When the client is
  given an IP literal it dials `check_port(peer, RELAY_PORT + 1)` =
  **21118** directly (client.rs:440–455), has no `signed_id_pk`, and
  `secure_connection` falls through: it sends an empty message and
  proceeds **unencrypted**. Symmetrically the host's direct listener
  calls `create_tcp_connection(…, secure = false, …)`, so
  `identity_handshake` is a no-op (`rendezvous_mediator.rs`
  `direct_server`, ~1354–1424; server.rs:213–260). The hash/challenge
  proof still never exposes the password itself, but on this path the
  proof (and then the whole desktop stream) has **no RustDesk-layer
  confidentiality or host authentication** — and the proof is a fast
  double-SHA256 with no slow KDF, so a captured proof is
  offline-brute-forceable against a weak permanent password.
  Consequences: (i) on the direct path, transport confidentiality must
  come from *our* tunnel (the runtime-proxy CONNECT path / tailnet),
  never from exposing 21118 raw; (ii) the laptop's permanent password
  must be long/random, since it is the only thing standing behind the
  proof; (iii) this is precisely today's `forward.sh` shape too — SSH
  supplies the encryption RustDesk direct mode lacks.
- **Fail-open downgrade exists on the relay path too:** if the signed
  pk is missing/invalid, the client logs and falls back to a
  non-secure connection rather than failing closed (client.rs
  `secure_connection`). A fleet relay must therefore be a *dumb* byte
  pipe that never strips or rewrites rendezvous messages; if we ever
  run our own `hbbs`, pin its key in the clients. (Not in the first
  build's path: direct mode has no rendezvous messages at all.)

## Findings (b) — Pre-warming: warm the tunnel, not the RustDesk session

Fleet side today:

- The broker *already* pre-warms: `serve.rs:592–606` spawns a thread
  that fills the pool for `PORT_LAPTOP_AGENT` at startup, through the
  same checkout accounting as requests. `TunnelPool` is per-port,
  `DEFAULT_POOL_SIZE = 50` (serve.rs, pool constants ~L66–L96),
  overflow = idle → grow → 300 ms wait → grow anyway.
- But pooled conns are wrapped as `HttpConn` and spent by
  `do_request` as HTTP request/response exchanges (serve.rs
  `Broker::open_conn` / `do_request`); the broker's wire protocol
  (`serve_session`, serve.rs:444ff; `client.rs` hello + JSON frames)
  has **no raw-stream mode**. A desktop needs a new capability, not a
  new pool.
- Below that layer everything needed already exists:
  `tunnel.rs:140–193` `connect_tunnel` returns a raw `TcpStream` from
  a CONNECT and reads the proxy response byte-wise precisely so
  payload bytes behind the headers are not eaten — i.e. it was built
  splice-safe. One explicit hazard: `tune()` applies
  `TUNNEL_READ_TIMEOUT = 660 s` (tunnel.rs:20–23, 195–199); a desktop
  splice must clear/raise that or long sessions die at 11 minutes —
  `forward.sh` sessions demonstrably run indefinitely once unmolested.

RustDesk side — which endpoint, and what a bare pre-connect does:

- On a TCP-only path the pool/splice target is the host's
  **direct-access port, 21118** — `direct-server = Y`,
  `direct-access-port` default 21118 (`RENDEZVOUS_PORT + 2`;
  rendezvous_mediator.rs `get_direct_port`/`direct_server`,
  ~1344–1424; advanced-settings doc above). Do not confuse it with
  `hbbs`'s WebSocket port, which is *also* numbered 21118 but lives on
  the server host, not the controlled laptop. The relay port 21117 is
  not a host endpoint at all — it is `hbbr`'s, and relay mode would
  require the host to dial out to a fleet-run `hbbr` and pair by uuid
  (option C below), which the direct port makes unnecessary.
- A bare TCP connect to 21118 is accepted and the host speaks first:
  `create_tcp_connection` (secure=false → handshake no-op) →
  `Connection::start` → `on_open` immediately sends `Hash{salt,
  challenge}` and waits. **No client protocol bytes are required
  first**; the Hash simply sits in the socket buffer until a real
  client is spliced in and reads it, and the client's first frame (an
  empty `Message` from its non-secure `secure_connection` fallthrough)
  is a no-op the host discards. So a pre-opened socket is
  protocol-valid to hand over.
- What breaks *naive* pre-warming (pool-50 for RustDesk sockets):
  1. **~30 s silent-idle death.** A connection that says nothing is
     closed when `last_recv_time` exceeds `SEC30` in the connection
     loop (connection.rs:1188–1191; comment at :85–89). The 180 s
     `LOGIN_GRACE` (connection.rs:90) only covers connections that
     are *talking* but not yet authorized. A pre-warmed idle socket
     therefore lives < ~30 s and needs constant churn.
  2. **Unauthorized-connection caps.** `MAX_UNAUTHORIZED_CONNS = 64`
     globally and `MAX_UNAUTHORIZED_CONNS_PER_ADDR = 16`
     (connection.rs:91–106, `admit_unauthorized` at :125ff), counted
     *before* the handshake, evicting the oldest on overflow. All
     fleet-forwarded connections appear from one address, so a pool
     of 50 is impossible and even ~16 idle pre-connects would crowd
     out real connection attempts.
  3. Each pre-connect is a real host-side `Connection`: visible in
     the host's connection manager, mints a fresh challenge, posts a
     connection audit record. Churn is user-visible on the laptop.
- **Conclusion:** the expensive, bursty part of starting a desktop
  today is tunnel establishment (CONNECT through the egress proxy;
  60 s handshake timeout budget in tunnel.rs:19, and seconds-long
  opens under burst per serve.rs's pool comments) — exactly what the
  existing pooled/preconnected tunnels already amortize. The
  RustDesk-layer connect on an already-warm tunnel is one local RTT
  plus the Hash the host sends unprompted. **Pre-warm tunnels (have
  it), splice on demand (build it); do not pre-warm RustDesk
  sockets.** If measurement later proves the RustDesk connect itself
  matters, a cache of 1–2 direct sockets refreshed every < 20 s is
  the maximum sane size — never 50.

## Findings (c) — Concurrency: one desktop, many viewers, zero isolation

A RustDesk host is a single controlled desktop with a multi-connection
server bolted on: `Server` owns one set of shared services (display,
audio, clipboard, input) and a map of `Connection`s (server.rs
`new()`, ~125–180); every authorized connection subscribes to the same
services and its input lands in the same session. So **yes, multiple
clients can be connected simultaneously — all viewing and controlling
the same desktop**, with interleaved mouse/keyboard and no locking,
partitioning, or per-client anything. That is a collaboration feature
and a footgun; fleet must not mistake "second connection" for "second
desktop".

Same shape elsewhere, for contrast:

- **KRDP** (`krdpserver`, KDE): a `SessionController` wraps each RDP
  connection, but every session captures the *same* running Plasma
  session (Portal or Plasma screencast of that session);
  `--virtual-monitor` adds a virtual output to that same session.
  Shared desktop, same as RustDesk.
- **x11vnc / TigerVNC scraping (`x0tigervncserver`)**: attach to the
  live X display `:0`; every viewer shares it (VNC "shared" is the
  natural mode).
- **TigerVNC virtual (`Xtigervnc`/`vncserver`) and xrdp+sesman**: the
  different model — the server *creates* a session per login
  (display `:N`, port `5900+N`; xrdp's sesman authenticates and starts
  a per-user X session, reconnect returns to that same session).
  Concurrency there means *separate* desktops, not shared control.

## Findings (d) — A desktop per connection

**RustDesk cannot do this.** It captures the session that exists —
on Linux, screen capture runs through PipeWire / `xdg-desktop-portal`
in a logged-in session (and the service can serve the login screen,
which is the part that keeps biting us) — and has no notion of
creating a session per connection. Any per-connection desktop has to
come from a different server or from compositor orchestration under
RustDesk-like tooling:

| Option | Per-connection desktop? | Shares | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CRD (`amd-crd`, running today) | One virtual X session per host instance — not per connection | Same `$HOME`/filesystem as the laptop | Already proves the shape we like: independent of physical login (our recurring blocker), but a second connection shares the one virtual desktop, and a shared Chrome profile dir means browser-instance contention. Google-brokered. |
| xrdp + sesman | Yes — per OS user, concurrent | `$HOME` if same user; isolate with distinct users + shared data dir | Mature, any RDP client, TCP 3389 splices through the fleet exactly like 21118 would. X11 sessions only — a shrinking target as Plasma goes Wayland-only. Per-connection browser profiles via separate `--user-data-dir`. |
| TigerVNC virtual | Yes — per display `:N`, allocatable on demand | Same as xrdp | Scriptable (fleet could allocate `:N` per request), X11-only, VNC protocol (RFB auth is weaker; rely on the fleet tunnel for confidentiality, as with RustDesk direct). |
| Nested/headless Wayland per connection | Yes — one `kwin_wayland --virtual` (or labwc/sway headless) instance per connection, KRDP or wayvnc inside it | `$HOME`; per-instance `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, portal, PipeWire | The forward-looking option and the only Wayland-native one. KRDP alone does **not** create login sessions — the fleet would orchestrate compositor instances (e.g. systemd user services) and hand out ports. Heaviest build; also the only one that survives Plasma dropping X11. |
| Separate X/Wayland session per *user* (display-manager) | Per user, not per connection | Same machine, real sessions | Middle ground: pre-provisioned 1–2 extra users with auto-login sessions, each running its own RustDesk/KRDP; connections-per-desktop still shared (see (c)). |

Sharing data across any of these is the easy half — same filesystem,
explicit browser profile dirs per connection
(`chromium --user-data-dir=…` per instance avoids profile-lock
contention) — the hard half is session lifecycle: who creates,
resizes, reaps, and logs into each desktop.

## Options

- **A. Status quo** — keep `forward.sh` (dedicated SSH forward) as the
  desktop path. Works, proven; but permanent second transport, no
  fleet pooling/preconnect, no services-map presence, SSH credential
  path maintained for one port.
- **B. Broker raw-splice to the direct port (recommended first
  build)** — fleet proxy gains a splice mode: sandbox-side listener
  on `127.0.0.1:21118`, each accept checks out a pooled tunnel
  (`connect_tunnel`) to laptop:21118 and copies bytes both ways.
  Secrets in broker: **none** (findings (a)). TCP-only compatible by
  construction. Keeps the working RustDesk physical-desktop experience
  and today's direct-IP client configuration, swapping only the pipe
  under it (SSH → fleet).
- **C. Fleet-run `hbbs`+`hbbr`, force relay** — the "real" RustDesk
  topology, and the only one with RustDesk-layer E2E encryption +
  host-key verification. Costs: running/pinning a rendezvous+relay,
  host registration traffic (21116 TCP/UDP) that our sandbox path
  can't carry (servers would have to live laptop-side or on a
  UDP-reachable host), force-relay config on both ends, and the
  fail-open downgrade caveat to police. Revisit if direct-path
  confidentiality ever has to come from RustDesk itself rather than
  the tunnel.
- **D. Replace RustDesk with KRDP/xrdp now** — premature: throws away
  the working physical-session path to solve the *virtual* desktop
  problem, which is separable and later (findings (d)).

## Recommendation — first build (smallest useful step)

Implement **B**, in this order:

1. **Register the service:** add a `rustdesk` entry for port **21118**
   to the fleet services table (`fleet-config` `Config::services`,
   currently 4799/4800/4801) so the broker's routing/hello map knows
   the port exists.
2. **Add a raw splice capability to `fleet-proxy`** (new broker
   capability beside `ProxyServe`, negotiated in the hello — proto-0
   brokers simply don't offer it):
   - client verb (name TBD, e.g. `fleet proxy desktop`) ensures the
     broker, then listens on sandbox `127.0.0.1:21118`;
   - per accepted connection: `pool_get(21118)` → bidirectional copy
     between the local socket and the tunnel stream; **no `HttpConn`
     wrapping, no token file, no request framing**; the tunnel is
     spent, never returned to the pool;
   - splice streams must **not** inherit `TUNNEL_READ_TIMEOUT`
     (660 s) — clear read/write timeouts on spliced conns
     (tunnel.rs `tune()` is HTTP-shaped; make it a caller choice).
3. **Secrets posture, stated in code comments and docs:** the broker
   and the splice hold no RustDesk credential of any kind; the
   permanent password is typed into the RustDesk client on the
   sandbox and its proof travels inside the spliced bytes; laptop
   21118 must remain reachable *only* through the fleet tunnel /
   loopback-class paths (direct mode has no transport encryption of
   its own — findings (a) caveat), and the laptop permanent password
   must be long and random.
4. **Keep `forward.sh` untouched as fallback** until the splice
   proves out; then retire it and the last routine use of the raw SSH
   forward with it.

Acceptance for the first build:

- Desktop session starts through the splice with the laptop's
  existing direct-IP RustDesk config; start latency measured against
  the `forward.sh` baseline (expect tunnel checkout, not tunnel
  establishment, to dominate).
- A session idles and works well past 30 minutes (no 660 s tunnel
  timeout, no mux-style freeze of the #5509 kind).
- Broker logs/config contain no RustDesk password or proof material
  (they structurally cannot — verify by inspection).
- Two simultaneous splices both land on the same laptop desktop —
  observed and documented as the shared-desktop semantics of
  findings (c), not treated as a bug.

Explicitly **not** in the first build: RustDesk-socket pre-warming
(findings (b) — at most a later, measured 1–2 socket / < 20 s-refresh
experiment), fleet-run `hbbs`/`hbbr` (option C), and per-connection
virtual desktops (findings (d)).

## Next steps

- [ ] Land the first build above as its own implementation issue
      (services-table entry + splice capability + timeout fix).
- [ ] Measure splice vs `forward.sh` connect latency and long-session
      stability; only then decide if a 1–2-socket RustDesk pre-warm
      experiment is worth its churn.
- [ ] Spike (separate design issue): per-connection virtual desktop —
      headless Wayland compositor per connection (`kwin_wayland
      --virtual` + KRDP) vs xrdp/TigerVNC-virtual as the X11 stopgap,
      with per-connection browser profile dirs; CRD/`amd-crd` stays
      the fallback until the spike proves out.
- [ ] Decide the end-state for option C (fleet `hbbs`/`hbbr`) if a
      future requirement wants RustDesk-layer encryption instead of
      tunnel-layer confidentiality.

items.title: projector(comments): pmp_comments is keyed by the bare GitHub numeric ID — an issue comment, a review comment and a review with the same ID silently overwrite each other

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

items.body:
## Problem

`pmp_comments` is keyed by the bare GitHub numeric ID alone, but the projector writes **three different kinds of GitHub objects** into that one table — issue comments, PR review comments, and PR reviews — and GitHub assigns those IDs from **independent sequences per object type**. The same number can therefore denote an issue comment and a review on the same (or different) items, and when it does, the second object silently **replaces** the first (main b3f6d2b2):

- `pm-stack/projector/schema.sql:47` — `id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, -- GitHub comment/review id`, no kind or repo qualifier.
- `pm-stack/projector/src/store.ts:207` — `upsertComment` is `ON CONFLICT(id) DO UPDATE SET` over every column including `ref`, `kind`, `body` and `deleted` (guarded only by `source_updated_at >=`, which a later-created colliding object passes).
- Every writer passes the raw per-type ID: webhook `commentCommon` (`src/projector.ts:80`, `String(c.id)`), the delete paths (`src/projector.ts:159` and `:213`, `markCommentDeleted(String(comment.id))` — a delete for one kind can tombstone another kind's row), and reconciliation (`src/reconcile.ts:76` issue/review comments, `:116` reviews, both `String(...id)`).

The unified activity stream (schema view `pmp_v_subject_activity`, `getCommentsForSubject`) then shows the surviving object and has lost the other one — no error anywhere, and reconciliation re-derives the same collision on every poll.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-projector/probe.ts`, real `store.upsertComment`/`getComments` against an in-memory libSQL DB migrated from the real schema.sql, main b3f6d2b2): upsert an `issue_comment` with id `424242` (created 2026-01-01), then upsert a `review` with the same id `424242` (created 2026-01-02):

```text
collision: rows=1 kinds=review bodies=review body
pmp_comments total rows = 1
```

The issue-comment row is gone — overwritten in place by the review, including its `ref` and `kind`. (The fixtures hint the namespaces were kept apart by hand: `fixtures/03-issue-comment.json` uses id 9001, `05-pr-review.json` 10001, `06-pr-review-comment.json` 11001.)

## Why it matters

The projector's whole purpose is a trustworthy unified comment/activity projection across the four repos (aggregator requirement #2). A cross-kind ID collision silently drops a real comment or review from every subject view and can cross-wire a deletion onto the wrong object. Because the monotonic guard compares `source_updated_at`, the corruption sticks: re-delivering the overwritten object's webhook is a no-op duplicate or loses the guard comparison, so the lost row does not heal itself.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Comment identity distinguishes the object kind (e.g. a composite key or a kind-qualified ID) at the schema level and in `upsertComment` / `markCommentDeleted`, so an issue comment, a review comment, and a review with the same numeric ID coexist as three rows.
- [ ] A delete event for one kind never tombstones a row of another kind.
- [ ] Store/projector tests pin the same-ID-different-kind case for all three kinds, plus the cross-kind delete case.
- [ ] Existing rows and the read model (`getComments`, `getCommentsForSubject`, `pmp_v_subject_activity`) keep working; the migration path for an existing database is stated in the PR (the DB is documented as disposable/rebuildable in schema.sql, if that is the chosen route).

Distinct from #2455 (deleted comments resurrected by stale upserts — the monotonic guard's key, not the primary key's namespace) and #2456 (failed webhook deliveries unretryable — the deliveries table, not comments).

items.title: infra: repo-queue PostgREST timeout: global failures lane-visible again — recurrence after #6450 closed (2026-11-06 21:15-21:31Z)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: priority/critical
labels.description: Drop everything: main broken, security exposure, repo-wide outage

items.body:
# infra: repo-queue PostgREST `timeout: global` failures are lane-visible again — recurrence after #6450 closed (2026-11-06 ~21:15–21:31Z)

## Evidence (lane code-w shift, 2026-11-06)

Five consecutive `fleet queue` calls failed with the same signature, exit 4:

- `fleet queue health --queue repo-health-code-pilot` — failed ~21:15Z, ~21:17Z, ~21:20Z, ~21:31Z (4 attempts)
- `fleet queue claim --queue repo-health-code-pilot --worker repo-worker-code --lane code-w --lease-seconds 2700` — failed ~21:24Z (1 attempt)

Every call: stderr `repo-queue: PostgREST request failed: timeout: global`, exit 4, each taking ~90s before failing. No task could be claimed; the lane-W shift ended with zero tasks worked. No claim was recorded by the failed claim call as far as the client can tell (the verb errored; atomic claim semantics + the 57014 rollback rationale in #6450 say a timed-out write rolled back — worth a broker-side confirm).

## Why this is a recurrence, not #6450 itself

#6450 closed COMPLETED 2026-11-06T17:44:35Z after PR #6584 deployed the posture (broker health cache 12s TTL, paced enqueues, shared backoff base 500ms ×2 cap 20s ×6 attempts on 57014/PGRST002). Its closing note recorded that in the post-deployment window (~17:48–17:51Z) timeouts still occurred at the DB but **no queue verb surfaced a failure** — calls were slow (~50s worst) but succeeded. Its close rule: the issue closes when a captured failure window proves the root cause, or the posture eliminates the windows.

This window breaks that: verbs are surfacing failures again, repeatedly, over 15+ minutes — either a longer/deeper window than backoff can absorb, a different failing leg (health aggregation was already the expensive verb: one `repo_queue_health` read cost 6,315 ms in the #6450 capture), or the sandbox client vintage (the #6450 note said installed client binaries update at the next fleet install/switch — the client-side backoff may not be live on this sandbox yet).

## Pointers

- Standing capture from #6450 arm (a): cron `queue-capture-6450` + broker failure-events log (`~/.local/state/queue-broker/failure-events.jsonl`) should have this window — check `hidden_files/queue-capture-6450/captures/` for a failure capture covering 21:15–21:31Z and correlate the pg_stat delta.
- Related but distinct: #6616 (backoff `is_retryable` substring-matching can misclassify permanent errors as statement timeouts).
- Prior occurrences: #6450 (2026-11-06, closed), #5370 (2026-11-04, closed).

## Acceptance

- The 21:15–21:31Z window is attributed from the capture stream (failing verb + DB-side cause), or a broker/client fix ships that makes this window class non-lane-visible, with the verification recorded here.
- Confirm no orphan claim was left by the failed 21:24Z claim call (task claimed by repo-worker-code / lane code-w with no checkpoint would be the tell).

items.title: chore(jules): complete decommission follow-up wiring (code#5098)
items.body: Completes the recorded follow-up wiring pass for the Jules decommission (code#5098) — the scope the main decommission PR (code#5111) deliberately left for a separate pass. Drew's ruling: full decommission, with every removal carrying a roughly equivalent replacement (the equivalence constraint from #5098). Opened as the app; **not merged** — returning for review. ## Removals (every item verified present before removal) **Packages — `pkgs/jules/`, `pkgs/jules-fleet/`, `pkgs/jules-merge/` deleted**, with their wiring in `nixos/environment/default.nix`: the three `callPackage` definitions (plus their comment blocks) and the `jules` / `jules-fleet` / `jules-merge` entries in `environment.systemPackages`. Also trimmed: the `gemini-cli` install comment that cited the `gemini-cli-extensions/jules` extension as a reason for the binary (gemini-cli itself stays — upstream is alive). **Aggregator — `pm-stack/aggregator/src/sources/jules.ts` deleted** (the keeper-state → SessionFeedEntry mapper), and its wiring: - `scripts/collect-fleet-feed.ts`: the Jules collection block (state read, session mapping into attention + registry, `julesSummary`, the `julesSummary` section status), the `JULES_STATE_PATH` env override, the summary-line totals clause, and `supervisionNotes()` — the keeper-annotation reader over the same state file (its only writer was the deleted jules-review cron; the file has been frozen since 2026-11-03T19:42Z). - `src/feed.ts`: the `julesSummary` feed field. `src/model.ts`: the `JulesSummary` type. `src/health.ts`: the `julesSummary` feed-health section. - `src/sources/live.ts`: the "Jules" row in the board's source-coverage list. - `src/sources/fixtures.ts`: the jules fixture session + fixture coverage row (fixtures mirror the live source set). - `src/actions.ts`: `"jules"` removed from `SESSION_SOURCES` (no new dashboard session actions can target the retired source); routing comment updated. - `src/render.ts`: the keeper-mediated branch of `sessionVerbSupport` (jules records now get no session controls, like any source with no control channel). - Docs/comments describing live wiring updated: aggregator README (sources, registry, routing, file/test maps), `src/registry.ts`, `src/server.ts`, `src/snapshots.ts`, `src/project-config.ts` (project intro), root `AGENTS.md` (schedule-surface enumeration). **Board impact (inspected live before the change):** every fresh feed still embeds the frozen keeper snapshot — the coverage list shows a "Jules" row ("via the keeper's state (jules-review) · 4 tracked now · last keeper run 2026-11-03T19:37:30Z") and 4 Jules session cards sit in attention/registry in `AWAITING_USER_FEEDBACK` state. All four sessions were in fact concluded via the API during the decommission, and the keeper cron is deleted, so that state could never move again. After this change the coverage row, the cards, and the feed's `julesSummary` section are gone; OpenCode (sandbox/laptop) and Muse sources are untouched. Jules records already merged into the aggregator's durable registry store remain there as history (runtime data; the store retains records after they expire out of the attention feed by design) and still render on /sessions — now without action controls. **`pkgs/agent-backup/backup.sh`**: `$HOME/.config/jules/api-key` removed from the snapshot CANDIDATES list (the file it named was trashed in the decommission). **NixOS refs**: `nixos/agent-auth/default.nix` — the `agent-auth/jules-api-key` sops declaration (it decrypted `google.jules-api-key` into /run/secrets for a loader code#5111 already removed) plus its header/bullet comments; `nixos/desktop/default.nix` import comment; `nixos/services/pm-stack/default.nix` — the fleet-feed-collector's `JULES_STATE_PATH` env (it pointed the collector at the keeper state file). **Secrets layer**: `google.jules-api-key` and `google.jules-oauth-creds` **deleted from Bitwarden Secrets Manager** (by name; `jules-oauth-creds` had no consumer anywhere in the repo), and their entries removed from `secrets/sops/common/bws.yaml` with `sops unset` (the file still decrypts; MAC valid). `lib/bws-to-sops.sh` mirrors every vault secret, so the vault deletion is what makes the mirror removal durable; its two header-comment examples that used `google.jules-api-key` now use `muse.sdk-token`. Noted while there: the committed mirror was stale — the vault holds ~35 secrets the mirror predates (incl. the `supabase.muse-dev*` / `supabase.muse-dev2.*` sets). A general re-sync is unrelated housekeeping and is deliberately NOT in this PR. ## Equivalence (Drew's constraint, per item) - Packages + NixOS wiring: the Jules CLI/fleet/merge tools' work — dispatch, supervision, merge shepherding — is done by the OpenCode lanes + pm-dispatch machinery that replaced them in the main decommission (opencode-daily-top-issue, opencode-bolt-palette, the orchestration pass). No capability is lost. - Aggregator source: the board's session supervision/attention function is carried by the OpenCode sources + pm-dispatch annotations; the Jules panel showed only frozen, concluded sessions. No capability is lost. - agent-backup entry, sops declaration, Bitwarden secrets: pure residue — the credential and its consumers are gone. No capability is lost. ## Kept by design (not residue) - `jules.yml` filename, the `jules` label, and the label machinery in `main-broken.yml` / `repo-sweeper.yml` / `agents.yml` / `nix-ci.yml` / `actionlint.yaml` / `ci-policy.md`: the pm-dispatch hub's kept names (established 2026-11-03). The `jules-daily-*.yml` OpenCode-era workflow names likewise stay, as does the Bolt/Palette prompts' `.jules/` journal-directory convention. ## Remaining `jules` grep hits (tree-wide, excluding .git) — all disclosed Aggregator code kept deliberately as **historical-data tolerance** (stored records and feeds published before the retirement still parse, group, and label correctly; none of it produces or feeds Jules data): - `src/model.ts`: `"jules"` in the `SessionSource` / `OrchestrationSource` unions + the source label, and doc comments naming the id forms (`jules:`, supervision-note provenance). - `src/derive.ts`: the `jules:` tier-item id prefix, and the rule that Jules questions never escalate to Drew (protects against stale published items). - `src/registry.ts`: the `agentIdentityOf` jules branch + the `keeper` standing author identity (they label historical records/comments). - `src/render.ts`: `"jules"` in `REGISTRY_SOURCE_ORDER` (grouping of stored records). `src/work-items.ts`: id-form comment. - `src/program.ts` and `src/project-config.ts` (program/editorial records): historical program text. Tests: the v1 contract-corpus JSONs (historical captures — the contract they pin), `registry-view` / `slice3` record-data tests of the tolerance paths above, `slice2`'s keeper-question tiering test, `actions` / `boot` tests that now pin the RETIRED behavior (no jules coverage entry, no keeper-mediated controls, jules no longer a valid action source), and label strings in `orchestration` / `board-in-flight` fixtures. Documents (historical records, not live wiring): `doc/agent-stack-notes.md`, `doc/fleet-schedule-registry.md` (Surface 3 already marked retired), the dated `doc/2026-*` report/design docs, `planning/roadmaps/*.md`, `ROADMAP.md`, `.opencode/instructions/mcpx.md` (an example env name), and the mcpx skill docs (`.agents/skills`, `.opencode/skills`, `pkgs/mcpx/plugin/...`) that mention Jules as an example agent. ## Proof - Aggregator: `bun test` — **1563 pass / 2 fail**; the 2 failures are the pre-existing `health surface counts the inbox (#1282 slice 1)` pair, failing identically on unmodified main (verified at baseline before any edit). `bunx tsc --noEmit` — only the pre-existing `src/item-history.ts` GhKind error (also at baseline). `bun run contract:check` — passed. - Collector run end-to-end against an empty HOME: exit 0; the emitted feed contains no jules keys or sections. - Nix: `nix eval .#nixosConfigurations.amd.config.system.build.toplevel.drvPath` evaluates clean; `nix build .#nixosConfigurations.amd.config.home-manager.users.user.home.activationPackage` built green. - `grep -ri jules --include="*.nix"` over the tree: zero hits. --- Open in [code]smith · Need help on this PR? Tag @codesmith-bot with what you need.

items.body:
# Project Management book — fifth house book, coverage audit, sidelines, Space

Programme tracking issue for the PM-BOOK lane (Drew's directive, 2026-11-23 ~18:29 CST). Built per the bookwright skill (v5): survey before structure, structure before prose, mechanical coverage audit before "done".

## The deliverable

A fifth book, **Project Management** (the project is still called "PM stack" in conversation; the book covers the wider concept), in `pkgs/pm-stack/docs/` beside the subject, matching the form of the four existing books (mcpx exemplar; fleet, atlas, id), joining the repo's single Pages deploy under its own subpath.

## Completion test (Drew's words)

> "You'll know the book is done when that's true": **every worker in the estate and every Turso database is covered in the PM book or in one or more of the four pre-existing books.**

The coverage ledger below is the test's evidence. It starts from the #13844 Turso→D1 audit estate list (50 DBs) and a fresh census of Cloudflare workers/doors from the repo, verified against live surfaces where the repo's tooling allows.

## Coverage ledger

_To be filled by the census slice: every worker and every Turso DB, each mapped to its covering book + chapter. Gaps close in the PM book by default, or in the owning book (fleet/atlas/id/mcpx) via the sidelines / follow-on chapter PRs._

## PM book scope (census the real systems; this list is the floor, not the ceiling)

- Everything the PM stack website has now, page by page: the aggregator + console (routes/pages, health/quota/usage views, the question sets).
- The half-used PM apps it integrates: Kaneo (confirmed — incl. the Kaneo PM bot) and every other app the census finds (Grist and the rest), what each is, how it's wired, how much is actually used.
- The Android app push-notification system end to end (the website pushes itself, event-driven at detection: outage + waiting-on-Drew classes, the section-risk class from #8882, the answer-writes-back mechanic).
- Roadmap/prioritisation mechanics: major initiatives, projects, epics, aggregators — what each type is, roll-up, prioritisation, answer-back flows.
- The queue systems and multiple dispatch methods from the PM perspective — overlap with the fleet book is fine; describe from this angle and link to the fleet book's documents.
- Bridge: light coverage here; its durable home is the fleet book + a `fleet` subcommand (follow-up issue filed by this programme). The standalone bridge build runs separately (pkgs/message-bridge) — coordinate, don't rebuild.
- The PM stack's own model dependencies (embedding models and any others).

items.title: Queue/lane design rules: no by-id blocking by default, optional platform selector, triage separate from fixes
items.body:
Drew's design rules for the queue/lane machinery, dictated 2026-11-09 20:22 CST after tonight's by-id claim fixes and lane-UUID registrations. These govern how lanes, the broker/claimant, and queue items are shaped.

## Rule 1 — No blocking by ID by default
Lanes must not need to block or claim by task ID in the regular queue flow. ID-targeted claims stay available for specific cases (e.g., reviving one specific parked handoff, as done tonight for task 11214), but they are the exception tool, never the default mechanism a lane depends on to get work.

## Rule 2 — No platform required; coarse selector allowed
A work item must not need a platform set on it. Provide an optional coarse selector — "use OpenChamber" or "use Muse" — that constrains which family may take the item without naming a specific lane. Default (no selector): either family's lanes may take it.

## Rule 3 — Triage is a separate step from fix work
Muse lanes work their own fixes. Triage is its own task/step, not something mixed ad hoc into fix work: a lane picking up a batch of tickets (Drew's example: 5) triages the ones that need triage as that separate step, and works fixes for the ones already triaged. (Batch size read as illustrative pending Drew's confirmation.)

## Acceptance
- The claimant/broker default flow demonstrably claims and launches regular queue work with no ID-targeted claims involved.
- The queue item schema shows platform/selector optional, with the two coarse values working end-to-end.
- Lane/sweep definitions show triage as a distinct step from fix work in the Muse lanes' flow.

items.title: feat(aggregator): audit event v2 — integrity + durable retry (#3322 slice A)
items.body: Implements issue #3322 slice A (queue task 8696): the #1739 event stream in `pm-stack/aggregator` becomes an audit v2 record. ## What changed - **Versioned v2 audit records** (`src/events.ts`): every stored record carries a stable id, separate event (`at`) and ingest (`ingestedAt`) timestamps, actor attribution with explicit confidence (`authenticated` only when asserted; pre-SSO/unknown marked, never upgraded), and source identity + optional link. v1 field names (`kind` = action, `ref` = object) are kept so all existing writers/readers work unchanged. - **v1 dual-read**: v1 store files load with deterministic migration ids (`migratedFromVersion: 1`, attribution `unknown`) and are rewritten as v2 on the next persist. Tested. - **Append-only corrections**: `recordCorrection` adds a separate attributable `correction` record naming its target (`corrects`); stored records are never edited in place. - **Integrity**: records are hash-linked (`prevHash`/`hash`, sha256 over canonical fields). `verifyEventChain` + `EventsStore.health()` detect a silently edited field, a re-stamped hash, or a deleted middle record; retention pruning keeps the last pruned hash as the chain anchor so pruned chains still verify. A tampered file loads with a loud integrity warning, surfaced via health — and `/api/events.json` now rides the health surface (pending retries + integrity verdict) along with the stream. - **Durable retry**: a failed append is persisted to `.outbox.jsonl` before the error is rethrown (fire-and-forget semantics unchanged), and the outbox is flushed — merged by stable id, then cleared — on load and on every subsequent append. No more silent "event lost". Slice B (backup/restore exercise + retention/archive finalization) is NOT here — it stays blocked on the #1258 storage decision, per the issue split. ## Tests - `bun test test/events.test.ts test/orchestration.test.ts` — 58 pass (22 events tests incl. 6 new v2 tests plus 3 Codex re-review regression tests: audit fields/hash link, asserted-attribution rejection, v1 migration, tamper detection, corrections, retry-outbox merge). - Full aggregator suite on the laptop worktree: 1383 pass with 2 unrelated failures also present independent of this change (a timing-flaky snapshot-lock concurrency test, which passes standalone 23/23, and a `web-push` module error from the fresh worktree before `bun install`). - `bunx tsc --noEmit`: no errors in the touched files (one pre-existing error in `test/overview.test.ts` remains). ## Codex re-review fixes (`621f790d8`, task 8696 resume) All three findings from the Codex review of `9c4a86a1` were verified real and are fixed, each with a regression test and a reply on its thread: - **P1 — outbox cleared before durable persist:** `flushOutbox()` now clears the outbox only after a successful `persist()` of everything it held; a pending record already in memory still triggers that persist, and a failing persist leaves the outbox in place. - **P2 — re-stamp erased integrity failures:** `persist()` refuses to write over a chain that failed verification (load-time verdict or persist-time re-check). The on-disk evidence stays byte-identical, the refused record waits in the retry outbox, and `health()` keeps reporting the violation until a human repairs the store. - **P2 — damaged v2 record migrated as v1:** legacy migration is gated on the file version (`{version: 1}` files only); a malformed row in a v2 file now takes the quarantine path with its bytes preserved. Refs #3322 (does not close it — slice B remains). --- Open in [code]smith · Need help on this PR? Tag @codesmith-bot with what you need.

- 7/200 DISPOSITION (not_planned/duplicate — incl. 4 "Scheduled Bolt" bot issues).

items.title: mcpx: a principal per surface and a permission per operation, declared permissively

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/m
labels.description: Medium: expected under 1 day of work

labels.name: meta/enriched

items.body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#298 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #253

## Summary

The daemon has no notion of *who* is calling. That is deliberate and documented
three times over — "the API is unauthenticated, so the network it is on is the
access control" (`internal/daemon/server.go:214`), "the socket's file
permissions are the access control" (`internal/daemon/origin.go:13`), "Every
endpoint is unauthenticated" (`internal/api/openapi.go:40`) — and for a daemon
on a unix socket it is the right model.

This issue is the **authorisation model**: one notion of a principal that each
surface can construct, and a permission declared on each operation. Built
permissively, in the same spirit as #253: every principal resolves to the owner,
every permission check answers yes, and the daemon behaves exactly as it does
today. What the work buys is that the *vocabulary exists* and is declared in one
place, so a future surface has something to populate and a future policy has
something to constrain.

**This blocks nothing.** No surface, transport or feature waits on it. An
unauthenticated local daemon is a complete answer and stays one. Ordered behind
#253 so the auth work proceeds in one line rather than two.

## Original notes

> security is just off the table right now, there's no blocker for adding
> security, there's no blocker for not having auth. just dont mix auth with
> other things in issues

Raised after an earlier draft of this issue framed itself as a precondition for
remote surfaces. It is not one, and the framing was wrong.

## Current state

**Unauthenticated by design, and consistently so.** Three separate places state
the model in the same terms, which indicates a decision rather than a drift. The
TCP listener's host is deliberately not defaulted
(`internal/daemon/server.go:216-220`): "that has to be somebody's decision
rather than a default." The daemon will bind a port and declines to guess you
meant to expose it.

**The peer uid is available and unread.** A unix socket connection carries peer
credentials (`SO_PEERCRED` / `LOCAL_PEERCRED`). mcpx never looks. "Which local
user is calling" is a principal obtainable today for free.

**The ops table is the asset.** Every operation is declared once in
`internal/api/ops*.go`, and that declaration drives the CLI command, the MCP
tool and the OpenAPI operation. #114 names this as the project's own precedent —
"one declaration should drive every surface". A permission attached there is
enforced everywhere by construction, including on surfaces that do not exist
yet.

**What is adjacent and is not this.** #253 is the authorization *interface*
(OAuth, resource server, 61 conformance rows). #300 is real credential
validation, behind #253. #240 and #205 are configured upstream auth never being
applied — mcpx as a client, the opposite direction. #204 is `Origin` validation,
a browser-threat defence, not authentication. #185 is a settings ceiling a
caller may lower but not raise — the same *shape* as a permission and worth
sharing machinery with.

## Approaches

### Approach A — least recommended: a principal only when a surface needs one

Leave it until ssh or a browser surface lands, then add identity to that
surface.

This is how a codebase ends with four authentication systems: each surface
invents a principal because none existed when it was written. The cost of
declaring the vocabulary now is small precisely *because* nothing depends on it
— there is no migration, no compatibility surface and no behaviour to preserve.
Doing it later means doing it four times, against live surfaces.

### Approach B — middle: principals now, permissions when needed

Construct a principal per surface, carry it through, and defer the permission
declarations.

Half the value for most of the work. A principal nothing consults is a field
that rots; without a permission to check it against, nothing exercises it and it
will be wrong by the time it matters.

### Approach C — recommended: both, permissively, and a decision that is always "yes" but always *recorded*

**1. Every surface constructs a principal.** One internal notion, built from
what each transport natively knows:

| surface | principal from |
| --- | --- |
| unix socket | peer credentials — the uid, available today, read nowhere |
| loopback TCP | nothing native; explicit configuration, or anonymous |
| ssh (#85) | the authenticated key |
| browser (#174) | a session, alongside #204's `Origin` check |
| plugin (#82) | a declared plugin identity rather than ambient trust |

**2. Every operation declares a permission.** A field on the ops-table entry,
checked at the one place all surfaces funnel through. Default policy: the
socket's owner gets everything, anonymous gets everything, and **the check
always returns yes**. Behaviour is identical to today.

**3. The decision is recorded even though it is always yes.** This is the piece
that makes the permissive stage worth shipping rather than merely harmless.
With principals constructed and permissions declared, mcpx can answer "what
would a policy have refused?" from real traffic, before any policy exists. That
is the same dry-run property #300 wants for credential checks, and the two
should share one mechanism.

What this deliberately does **not** do: define a policy file format, decide
which scopes may grant, or enforce anything. Those are a later issue, and they
are the parts with actual risk.

## Open questions

- Is the permission vocabulary per-operation, or a small set of tiers
  (`read`/`run`/`admin`) operations are tagged with? Tiers are comprehensible
  and coarse; per-operation becomes a 200-row table nobody reads. Leaning tiers.
- Does a *tool call* carry a permission, or only mcpx's own operations? Upstream
  tools are not in the ops table, and they are the interesting surface. Possibly
  #114's tool views are the natural grant unit.
- Does the principal belong in the request context, or in the existing session
  notion? There is already a session key (`_meta["ai.opencode/sessionID"]`,
  #211); a principal is not a session but they travel together.
- Should `mcpx doctor` report "authorisation: permissive" so nobody deploys
  believing otherwise? Same hazard #300 flags for the credential interface, and
  the same answer: yes, loudly.
- Shared machinery with #185's clamping — same ceiling shape, probably one
  implementation.
- Does the socket peer uid distinguish anything useful on a single-user laptop?
  Honestly, rarely. It matters for a shared host and for #255's elicitation
  storage concern, and it is nearly free, which is the whole argument.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease:** M for principals and the declaration field; S for the permissive check
and the decision log. The enforcement, policy format and config-chain
constraints are explicitly **out of scope** and belong to a later issue.
**Impact:** low and deferred — this is vocabulary, not capability. Worth doing
early only because it is cheap while nothing depends on it. **Blocks nothing.**

**Depends on / related:** **#253 (the auth interface — this is ordered behind
it)**, #300 (real credential validation — the sibling second stage, also behind
#253, also blocking nothing), #185 (clamped settings — same ceiling shape,
share machinery), #204 (Origin validation — adjacent, not a substitute), #240
and #205 (configured upstream auth never applied — mcpx as client, the other
direction), #255 (elicitation storage permissions — a case a principal would
make expressible), #82 (plugins as a principal), #114 (tool views as a possible
grant unit), #113 (the operation surface where a policy would be administered),
#174 (surfaces — each would supply a principal as it lands, none waits on this).

## Acceptance criteria

- A principal type exists that every surface (unix socket, TCP, HTTP) can construct, and a permission is declared per operation in one place.
- Built permissively: every principal resolves to the owner and every check answers yes — daemon behaviour is byte-for-byte unchanged for existing clients.
- The vocabulary is documented where the current unauthenticated model is stated (`server.go`, `origin.go`, `openapi.go`), superseding those comments.
- Tests pin the permissive behaviour so a future policy change is a deliberate diff, not an accident.
